Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask a question with reference to the proposed Long Sault dam, and before doing so it is necessary that I should read a letter that I have received from Washington. The letter is as follows:
Washington, February 13, 1911,

Reid, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Dr. Reid,-I am taking the liberty of writing you at length, advising you of the position I hhve taken in opposing the ' Long Sault Development Companies Bill,* now pending in both Houses here.
An investigation of the Bills pending in the interest of the Long Sault Development Company discloses the fact that the company is endeavouring to get legislation that will enable them to develop power south of the International boundary line entirely independent of and without the consent of the Canadian government. The original Malby Bill, introduced December 14, 1909, contained a provision that the authority thereby vested in the company would not be operative until the consent of the construction of the dams, canals and locks and other works of the proper authorities of the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada was obtained. This Bill was submitted to General 0. H. Ernst, the chairman of the American section of the International Waterways Commission, who has devoted about six years to the consideration of this great International waterways, for his opinion. He, with the other members of the American section, joined in the opinion that the co-operation of the two governments was essential and necessary and recommended a section to be attached to the Malby Bill, for the purpose of accomplishing that result, reading as follows:
* This Act shall not become operative until the government of the Dominion of Canada shall signify to the Secretary of State of the United States its consent to the construction of such dam and other structures; provided, that if said consent be not given within two years from the date of this Act, then this Act shall be null and void.'
Notwithstanding this proposition of the original Malby Bill and this .specific recommendation of the American section of the International Waterways Commission, the Bill finally reported by the Rivers and Harbours Committee and the Bill now pending in the Senate, both being identical-entirely omits any provision requiring the consent of the Dominion of Canada, It does contain a section which provides that the Long Sault Development Company shall be subiect to the provisions of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain relative to boundary waters, proclaimed May 13. 1910.
An examination of the treaty discloses the interesting fact that article IV which relates to dams, is subject to approval in accordance with the provisions of article VIII. Article VIII provides that a majority of the commissioners shall have power to render a decision and further provides that in case the commission is equally divided separate reports are to be made on each side by the commission to their own agreement and in that case, the governments are to endeavour to agree. But it is obvious that if they do not agree no result is reached, the result of which is that, if dams proposed to be built by the Long Sault Development Company are not approved by a majority of the commission equally decides, that as far as the Interna-

tional Waterways Commission is concerned the situation of the company is not in the slightest degree changed, because the provisions of the treaty with reference to the approval of the commissioners will have been exhausted without any definite result.
The pending Bill evidently anticipated this situation, because it not only omits all provisions requiring the approval of the Dominion of Canada to the construction of the dams, but expressly provides that the company is 'authorized to construct, maintain and operate for navigation, water-power and other purposes for a period of ninety-nine years, a dam or dams in so much of the St. Lawrence river as lies south of the International boundary line between the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada near Long Sault, Barnhart and Sheik Islands either independently or in connection with like works now erected or to he erected in so much of said river as lies north of said International boundary line.'
It discloses the specific and deliberate purpose of authorizing the Long Sault Development Company to build its dams south of the International boundary line without the consent or approval of the Dominion of Canada.
I strongly urge upon you to lay before parliament the above facts, and oblige,
Yours very truly,

I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if he has any further information in connection with this matter. If the facts as contained in this letter are as he understands them to be with reference to the situation at Washington, and if he has instructed Ambassador Bryce to protest against the Bill now before the United States Senate.

speechtext: I have heard only a part of the statement of Mr. Allison. For my part, I do not agree at all with some of his conclusions. We have made representations to the government at Washington and the correspondence will be brought down as soon as completed.

I wish to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) whether the treaty now being negotiated with the United States regarding Pelagic Sealing will require to be ratified by this House before it goes into operation or whether it will take effect without the concurrence or assent of this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This treaty will take effect without the concurrence or assent of this House, but it is our intention to bring down the treaty as soon as received and if parliament desires to express any opinion upon it it may do so.

iVIr. LENNOX. Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I would like to call the attention of the House to an error that occurred in some of the figures I presented yesterday. In doing so I think it is right that I should say that I expect it is my own fault, because I turned my back literally, not figuratively, upon the * Hansard ' reporters when speaking. I was addressing my particular friends on this side of the House, and so I did not give the members of the ' Hansard ' staff a fair opportunity of hearing what I was saying. The first is in reference to the product of Ontario farms in which I am made to say that it increased in two years $250,000,000. What I did say was that the annual product of Ontario farms now amounts to some $250,000,000. Then again there is an error in reference to the amount of American capital invested in Canada. I mentioned distinctly that there was $250,000,000 invested in Canadian industries by American manufacturers. In that connection, in the course of two or three sentences there are several errors. I will read what I said and as I have revised it now. Otherwise, as far as I have gone through the report it is satisfactory, but I have not got through it all yet. This is what I said:
Since 1868 we have doubled in population, we have enormous American industries planted in Canada representing $250,000,000. we have more than that number pf millions of dollars capital wanting to come to Canada, and halted by reason of the attitude of the government at the present time. The area of Canada under cultivation is ten times what is was in 1868; banking capital is ten times what it was; deposits in the banks are nearly thirty times what they were; our railway mileage is about twelve times what it was: and the freightage is about twelve times what it was in 1868.
I hope it will not be said at any future time, if it should turn out. that in the figures later on in the course of the report of my remarks yesterday there should he an error, that I adopt them because I do not refer to them now. As I have said, I have not had time to go over the whole of my speech yesterday and there may be errors later on, but these are important, and I desire to call the attention of the House to the correction.

I have to-day received from Vernon, B. C., the following telegram which with permission of the House I shall read :
Vernon, B.C., Feb. 16. Mr. Martin Burrell, M.P.,
Ottawa.
The bumble petition of the ratepayers and residents of the district, municipality of Coldstream, Vernon, British Columbia. Whereas the Dominion government is about

to introduce a Bill providing for reciprocity *with the United States of America on certain commodities under which are included fruit. And whereas the inhabitants of the said district municipality of Coldstream are dependent entirely on the fruit industry for their subsistence and the future prosperity of the district, we your petitioners desire to lay before the House of the Dominion parliament the views of the fruit growers of this district as hereunder set forward. Opinions may and do differ as to the relative merits of protection and free trade, but there can be no difference of opinion in the point that if protection is given at all it should be given equally to all interests according to the requirements. It seems . to be accepted that manufacturers are entitled to protection especially during the early years of any industry. So far as need of protection to the building up of an industry is concerned fruit growing stands in much greater need of protection than any manufactory as must be plain on the face of it to any one conversant with the conditions of this particular industry.
Is the hon. gentleman reading a telegram or a petition?
I am reading a telegram bearing on a matter of importance.
The matter has been referred to the Committee on Ways and Means.
I was going to read this as a petition, but there are not a sufficient number of names on it for a petition.
Petitions cannot be read in the House.
This is not a petition inasmuch as the technical conditions have not been complied with, there being only two signatures to it. I thought it was in order to bring it up on a motion to go into supply.
The matter has been referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and cannot be discussed.
I am in the hands of the House, and I would like to have an opinion on it.
I have no objection to allow the telegram being read, but the matter cannot be commented on now.
I do not think it is the intention of the hon. gentleman to discuss the matter.

I have no intention of discussing it ; I simply wish to read the telegram :
A manufactory can start production as soon as the plant is completed, an orchard after being laid out has to be tended for quite a number of years at a considerable outlay of capital before any return can be hoped for. The newer orchards of British Columbia planted in recent years and com-Mr. BURRELL.
prising an immense acreage are just now coming into bearing and the owners look to current conditions for marketing their fruit to advantage. No worse time as regards the fruit industry in this province could have been chosen to remove the duty on imported fruit. In ten years the fruit industry of British Columbia which is now in its infancy should be in a position to carry the battle of competition across the border having used che interval to build up its connections 'll the home market with the hope of the very moderate protection hitherto afforded. At the present time the home markets are mostly in the hands of the American producers who have the advantage of many years start, have organized thoroughly for the fight and have admittedly a distinct advantage over us in the cost of production. Even with the present protection it will be a long and uphill fight to get the home markets out of the hands of the Americans without it, the fight will be so long and uphill that many British Columbian producers will go under! Handicapped in this way in the home markets, our efforts to develop suffici-entlv to invade foreign territory are certain to fail for many years if not altogether. An enormous amount of capital has been invested in orchards in British Columbia during the past six years, the period during which the fruit industry has been strenuously promoted and the fruit growers looked to a continuance of the current conditions to enable them to realize interests in their invested capital out of which up to the present time it has been practically impossible to obtain any returns. We unanimously consider that the Dominion Houses of parliament should refuse to sanction the removal of the duty on fruit at the present time. There is no justifce in sacrificing the interests cf an infant industry for the benefit of a full grown industry which is in a very prosperous state under present conditions, and your petitioners are in duty bound will forever pray, &c.
JOHN KIDSON, Acting Reeve.
E. HENDERSON, Clerk.

Yesterday a question was raised which could not be disposed of with reference to my hon. friend from Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and a statement he made in the debate on the address. His statement referred to the Public Accounts, and as it was brought up yesterday and questioned, I thought that perhaps it was worth while to take the time of the House sufficiently long to rise to a solemn question of privilege, and just simply note the statement and make a remark with reference to it. The member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) in his address on November 22, said in reference to me :
He would not let the militia go out to drill; he saved several hundreds of thousands of dollars in that. He would not grant any money for the necessary repairs to public works, which from year to year go down, so that a dollar spent this year in repairs

may save ten dollars next year; he saved hundreds of thousands of dollars there.
Now, this is the part I particularly refer to :
Contrary to the statute, as I maintain, he did not that year provide a sinking fund to meet the national debt, saving 'hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of dollars there. That is the way he squared his accounts for the election year.
Some days afterwards the member for South Wellington on November 24, had his attention called to his error in figures in reference to the trade of the country, and he corrected that error. I then rose and said :

While the hon. gentleman is in a correcting mood, I will call his attention to page 96 where he is reported as having said:
Contrary to the statutes, as I maintain.
That is. myself.
-did not that year provide a sinking fund to meet the national debt, saving hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of dollars there.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) will look that up he will find that he is quite mistaken.
I have no correction to there.
Willing to let the statement go uncorrected.
So far as my knowledge goes, the statement is correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) does not follow the other side in refusing to correct even wrong statements.
I thought it was better to settle this question between the member for South Wellington and myself toy getting a statement from the Finance Department, and I, therefore, put upon the Order Paper the following question :
What was the amount legally required to be invested in the sinking fund for the fiscal years 1895 and 1896 respectively, and what was the amount actually invested in each of these years?
The answer given by Mr. Paterson for the Finance Minister was:
In. 1895, amount required and actually invested in sinking funds, $2,002,311.36; in 1896, amount required and actually invested in sinking funds, $2,005,287.52.
The answer of the Finance Department being of course that the amount required by the statute was so much, and that the amount invested was so much. I do not want to debate the question, but it is rather a grave charge against a Finance Minister to say that he tried to square his accounts by juggling with the sinking funds, a thing which under the statute he could not do; it would be an impossibility for him to do it.

I noticed the question that was placed on the Order Paper some time in November in regard to this matter, and the reply that was given by the Finance Department. I thought that the matter would probably have been brought up then, and I had a memorandum in regard to it which I cannot place my hand upon at this moment. I am satisfied that the words which I used in my remarks, ' contrary to the statute ', were not the appropriate words to describe what I meant. I find that the statute applies only to sinking funds on what are called guaranteed imperial loans. The sinking fund prescribed by statute is one per cent to be laid aside annually. There are other loans besides these, but I cannot give the amount of them now, nor the years, not having the memorandum. I can recollect one of them, of which the particulars were furnished in a return to this House-the loan of 1884 for $24,000,000. There was no statute, so far as I know, providing for a sinking fund on that loan; but it was the custom of the government to raise such a sinking fund. There were a great many other loans, negotiated by the late Conservative government. They finally decided for some reason best known to themselves to stop the sinking funds altogether on the new loans. They discontinued-through what I should have said instead of ' contrary to the statute ', was unbusinesslike methods or some such words, which would probably have better described the situation, as the statute applied only to the loans guaranteed by the imperial government. Now, my statement, in that aspect, is not so far wrong, because I think the saving by not having a sinking fund on all the later loans made by the Conservative government was from $500,000 to $700,000 a vear. This government also did not provide a sinking fund for a long period, but latterly I believe they have provided a sinking fund with all their loans. If the matter has caused my hon. friend from North Toronto any anxiety, or if he thinks I intended to cast any reflection upon him personally, I take this opportunity of entirely disavowing any such idea or intention. I now find that there was no statute applicable to the later loans. It was a mere_ custom to provide sinking funds, which I think should not have been discontinued, as it certainly resulted in a great saving of money.

Perhaps I may be allowed a single word. There is a great difference between criticising a man for issuing a loan without providing for a sinking fund along with it, and criticising a Finance Minister for failing, contrary to the statutes, to invest a sinking fund, in order to cover up a deficit. There is not a single word more to be said on my part in that respect. My hon. friend would have oc-

cupied a more frank position if he had at once said that he was wrong in that, and had done me an injustice. I have not been bothering about it, but such things are just as well not said. Now he is wrong again. He acknowledges that the Finance Minister whom he supports issued loans without putting on sinking funds. Has he been, ' contrary to the statutes ', juggling with funds and thereby covering up his deficits? My hon. friend then made the statement that the Finance Minister had since taken wiser advice and that with his later loans had sinking funds. He is mistaken there also.
I have been so informed by the Finance Department.
Then I may advise my hon. friend to get good information before he makes charges of that kind. They are not nice.

["I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned the matter, and I will furnish him with the reason for that change. I may say that in British Columbia, the western provinces, and the maritime provinces the overseers are all appointed by the federal government; I do not think there are any other overseers in those provinces except those appointed by the federal government, though there may be a few appointed by the provincial authorities. It was found advisable that we should have in Ontario our own officers to carry out our own laws and regulations. Formerly, all the officers were appointed by the federal authorities. But by a judgment which was rendered in 1898, it was decided that the beds of the rivers above the tide were the property of the provinces, and that the provinces had some rights in the fisheries, one of which was to issue licenses for catching fish. As a result of that judgment, most of the officers were kept on by the provincial authorities; we had, however, to maintain a limited number of our own officers. It was found, however, that the provincial officers were looking chiefly after the execution of the provincial regulations concerning the issuing of licenses, they were not supposed to carry out the federal regulations. It seemed proper, therefore, that the regulations passed by the federal authorities should be carried out by federal officers. I am not making any reflection upon the way the fisheries had been protected by the provincial officers, but they were not of course appointed to carry out our regulations. There were numerous complaints that our regulations were not properly enforced, and facts were reported to the department which rendered it advisable for us to appoint our own officers to look after the protection of the fisheries in pursuance of our own regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Several days ago we laid on the table a small sheet of supplementary estimates for the current year, containing several items of urgency to which I now call the attention of the committee. The items are four in number-one for Agriculture and Statistics, one for Immigration, one for the Naval Service, and one for the Department of Labour.
Exhibitions-further amount required, $100,-
000.

I am asking for this vote because of our participation in a Festival of Empire which is to be held at the Crystal Palace in London during the coming summer in connection with the coronation ceremonies and the colonial conference. This festival originated last year, and it was expected to have been held last year, but not nearly on so large a scale, as is now proposed. In consequence, however, of the death of His Majesty King Edward it was stopped and was postponed until this year. In view of the coronation and the colonial conference, the gentlemen in charge of this exhibition and festival have greatly enlarged their plans, and are proposing a most imposing and splendid celebration at the historic grounds of the Crystal Palace at Sydenham. We were invited to take part in it, and I went over the matter in London last spring, and formed a plan for a worthy representation of Canada at such an import-Mr. FOSTER
ant event. When I returned home I submitted it to my colleagues, and they approved of the suggestion that Canada could hardly be absent from such a festival, and that if we took part in it we should do so in a manner worthy of the country and worthy of the occasion. My exhibition commissioner has been proceeding with the plans. We had a little money to spend from the vote for this year, but we are now being dunned for obligations which we have incurred, and I am therefore obliged to ask for a prompt passage of this item to meet the obligations which we have already incurred or which will be incurred before the first of April next, when next year's appropriation will be available.
How does the minister propose to expend part of this money for which obligations have not already been incurred? The minister is now asking $100,000 and some money has already been expended.
Yes, not voted specifically for this exhibition, but out of the general vote for exhibitions for the year.
The minister is using money voted for exhibitions for this Festival of Empire?

Yes, it comes under the head of exhibitions. The vote of $120,000 is for exhibitions generally. Some of the money left over after we had done most of the work connected with the Brussels exhibition has been utilized for the preliminary work in connection with this exhibition. There are still some outstanding accounts in connection with the Brussels exhibition which have not been paid, as those rendering the accounts did not furnish sufficient information about them. Usually the accounts for different exhibitions overlap to a certain extent. As a matter of fact, during the current fiscal year we still have some accounts te pay for the Seattle exhibition of 1909-10.
What has the Brussels exhibition cost so far?

Apparently the minister has used money for another purpose than that for which it was voted, and has given the explanation that the government decided to take some of this money for another purpose other than that for which it was voted. If this policy were pursued there would be no limitation to the minister's power to spend money.

This vote for exhibitions is like a vote for running the Intercolonial railway or anything of that kind. We mention exhibitions generally, and if there is a new exhibition after the vote is given we hold ourselves free, if in the

judgment of the government it is thought best to take part in it, to utilize to a certain extent that money.
Was this exhibition in contemplation when the vote was taken last year?

The Festival of Empire of last year was under consideration and was provided for by this parliament. It was not proceeded with on account of the death of the King but was postponed until this coming summer. It is now being gone on with on a much larger scale. We in tended taking part in the Festival of Empire last year and as a matter of fact spent $4,000 or $5,000 in preliminary work on it.

If I understand it correctly, this $100,000 for which the minister is asking has all been spent, or will be spent, between now and March 31? How does it come that, though we voted $120,000 last session, he has exceeded that, and has spent $100,000 more?

The money has not been spent. We have not had it to spend. We have incurred obligations, I confess. The festival of last year was a small affair as compared with what is now proposed. We have been invited to take part in an affair planned on a much more magnificent scale at the time of the coronation of His Majesty the King, and the holding of the Colonial Conference. We feel it necessary that Canada should be worthily represented, and so have arranged to spend this $100,000 before the end of this fiscal year. This was not contemplated when the vote of $120,000 was asked last session.
How does the minister intend to spend $100,000 between now and the 31st March?

I have here full details. As I explained to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), these accounts of exhibitions lap over one year upon another. because we are not able to close up the accounts within the year. The following items are included in this proposed expenditure of $100,000:

Practically every dollar of this $100,000 has been spent?
As a matter of fact, none of it has been spent, for we have not the money.

But debts have been contracted, so that practically the money has been spent before parliament has voted it. Might as well have no parliament and let the ministers spend what money they like, for they spend it and then call on their supporters to vote it.

I explained all that. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that, if we had waited until this session opened to decide whether we should take part in this exhibition, it would be a physical impossibility to get ready for it. We had to assume the responsibility, and we ask parliament to support us in that action. I venture to think that hon. gentlemen opposite who have seen the work done on the part of Canada at these various exhibitions will upheld us in deciding to take part in this festival at the heart of the empire on the coming auspicious occasion.
It would help us more if you would tell us what you are going to do.

That is what I am trying to do. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) interrupting, I shall be glad to go on. But my explanations are too satisfactory, ap-,ny explanations are too satisfactory, apparently-hon. gentlemen opposite do not want to hear them. I want to go on with the explanation-
Get at it.

I am not going to let hon. gentlemen opposite have the pleasure of asking for explanations without giving them the answer. Does my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) wish me to read again these figures that I have given ?
I understood that these were mere details of boxing and housing. But what is it going to be? Tell us so that we may know where we are.

The Festival of Empire is an organization started on a comparatively small scale last year under the auspices of

a committee authorized by the King and under the patronage of the British government, and with Lord Plymouth as chairman. That organization planned a festival of empire for last year, in which the overseas dominions were invited to participate. They planned a great pageant of the whole empire under the management of Mr. Las-celles, well known in Canada as the successful director of the pageants in the Tercentenary at Quebec. While the arrangements otherwise were on a comparatively moderate scale, the pageant was a large one. This year they invited us to undertake exhibition work on a much larger scale, to do what we have done at many international exhibitions-put up a special Canadian building and display in it a thoroughly representative exhibit of Canada's resources, industries and institutions. That we propose to do. We intend to have a building on the grounds at the Crystal Palace, to take the form of a facsimile of these parliament buildings, to show to the world the parliament buildings of Canada as a part of our exhibit.
And have the members there?

Those who will visit the place will be made very welcome, and I think it wdll be well that many of them should he there. I am glad to know that many members on the other side of the House who have seen Canada's exhibits at different foreign exhibitions have, in unstinted measure, praised the work done by the exhibition commissioner of Canada and his staff, and have recognized the value to the country of these exhibits of our progress and industry.
Ycu are getting away off. Confine yourself to the Crystal Palace.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) need not be so captious. We know how jocular and facetious he can be, but I think that he might give serious attention to this important part of the country's business.
That's what we want-

If the hon. gentleman wants it, then let him allow iit. He is the first man in the House to resent any interruption himself when he is on his feet, and he should have a little more regard for the rights of others. Hon. members are aware that the exhibit at the Crystal Palace will be visited by hundreds and thousands, probably millions, of people, and that if Canada is going to be worthily represented, we must have a complete assortment of her products, hex industries, and something to show her progress. This cannot* be done without a considerable expenditure of money. I am willing to take the Mr. FISHER.
full responsibility of asking parliament to grant this money, because I have seen year after year the beneficial effects of these exhibits abroad, and am sure that the money will be expended to the advantage of Canada. I understand from my hon. friend that the other self-governing dominions are taking part, and are contributing; I hope so, because I am confident that Canada will be able to shine in comparison with any other part of the empire. That is one reason why after a good deal of hesitation and consultation with my exhibition commissioner, I authorized him to proceed to build, as nearly as possible, a facsimile of this central parliamentary block. We are all proud of our parliament buildings, as an example of Canadian architecture and construction. I think that everybody who comes to Ottawa is charmed with the appearance, with the magnificence and with the site of our parliament buildings here; and consequently, strangers who visit that festival in the Crystal Palace, will admire the Canadian building. The building will be so arranged as to contain the exhibits inside, these exhibits will be a modification and augmentation of what we have had at Brussels and other places, and will be renewed so as to be entirely up to date. We will transfer a considerable part of the exhibits from Brussels to the Crystal Palace, and others will be added.

I understand the minister to say that the proposed building will be a facsimile of the parliament buildings. In that case, does he propose to have a restaurant installed in it, with all the other conveniences ?
No, we never have a restaurant in our exhibition buildings; we leave that to other contractors, and people who get privileges to establish restaurants on the ground.
Will there he a bar ?

No bar there. I may inform hon. gentlemen opposite, that if they go there to find a bar, they will have to go elsewhere. The grounds are laid out so as to form practically a circle occupied by the buildings. The grounds are very extensive, covering, I think, some seventy or eighty acres of land. They are to be laid out so that the buildings of the different parts of the empire will form a circle; and the proposition is to have a railroad track going around these grounds, and touching at the buildings of the different parts of the empire.
Will that be a mono rail ?
I do not know.

If the minister is going to make the illusion perfect with a facsimile

of this building, I would suggest that he make a mound of something like our parliament hill, and have some streams of water on each side to represent the rivers. It would not cost much, and it would make the illusion perfect.

We have not the control of the grounds of the Crystal Palace; we have a certain space given us on which to erect o-ur building, but the general commission will manage the laying out of the grounds in general; we have no control, outside of what is given to us. But I can assure the House that the building will be so placed as to give a good impression of its grandeur, and its architectural beauty. In connection with the festival, there will be a great pageant of the history of the empire, for which there is provision on the grounds of the Crystal Palace, and which is to be managed by Mr. Frank Lascelles, who managed the Tercentenary celebration of Quebec, and who has just returned from South Africa, where he managed the celebration in connection with the opening of the South African parliament. The whole exhibition, as I have said, is under the control of this commission of which Lord Plymouth is chairman, and is under the immediate patronage of the King and of the imperial government. I believe the occasion is one in which Canada ought to be well represented, and I think that from the skill and well known capacity of the exhibition commissioner for Canada, who has now had twelve years experience in this work, he will be able to make a good representation of Canada and one which will be a splendid advertisement for this country.

Usually when we vote money, the object is stated and the money is specifically voted for that purpose. In this case, before there is comparatively any money voted, the money has been expended, or contractd for, although it could not be regarded as a case of emergency requiring a Governor General's warrant. Yet the minister goes on and expends money or contracts to expend the money and commits the country to obligations, and then comes and asks parliament to vote the money. I could not understand at first the meaning of the term ' Festival of Empire,' or what was the nature of this great pageant about which the minister has spoken, whether it was a kind of mardi gras procession, or a great feast. We do not know whether the greater part of this money will be consumed in pageantry, and very'little in the exhibition.

That is $10,000 for the grounds. How, there is another feature of this case, it is something which must have been foreseen, therefore it should have been provided for, by a vote, instead of by Governor Generals warrants. The minister admits in his own explanation that it was not a thing that could not be foreseen. Therefore, it ought to have been provided for, and if it was not provided for I respectfully submit that there was no justification for spending the money and therefore radically wrong. The minister says that we have from year to year voted money for exhibitions. This, according to his own showing, is not an exhibition ; it is a festival, a pageant, a show, but I presume that a few exhibition attachments have been tacked on to give it the semblance of an exhibition, so as to provide some justification for what would otherwise have been an improper and illegal expenditure of public money without that money having been voted. I am afraid that somebody is going to have a hippodrome as we have had them at Quebec, in South Africa, and in London. I am afraid this is a kind of a hippodrome business that the minister is trying to get up, and that he is going to carry on under the name of an exhibition. We are asked to vote $100,000, but whether it is worth the money I am not prepared to say. I would be better prepared to say if I saw it but I presume I will not have an opportunity of seeing it. It seems to me that we will get very little return from this expenditure of this money ; we keep a number of people who would otherwise be unemployed by the government, and who would, therefore, be obliged to resort to some other device for making a living. I do not think we are justified in going so far. We give these things high sounding names to make it appear that they are different from what they are. Is this a festival or is it not? If it is a festival it is not an exhibition. It is a mere pageant, it is not an exhibition, where there is likely to be a large number of people gathered together, but it is going to be given the semblance of an exhibition in order that we shall have some justification for the expenditure of this money. I think it is rather that than the usual expenditure of public money upon an exhibition where people will be benefited by what they see, and where their attention will be likely to be attracted to Canada and her industries. If I am correct we have an exhibition going in London all the time at which there are exhibits from all portions of the empire. Do we require a half a dozen of them, or is

this an addition to that, or is it something different from it? It must toe something different or otherwise we would hear something about it. But it seems to be another device to keep .an army of the unemployed spending the country's money, making displays, or exhibitions or festivals, or gatherings, or pageants, or something of that kind for which we must pay a lot of money, and from which expenditure it is very questionable whether we are getting anything like an adequate return. It seems to me that we are not very likely to get a proper return for this $100,-
000.

I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman at all. I am sorry that he has not attended any of these foreign exhibitions. He tells me that he has not, and I can, therefore, forgive to a certain extent what he says. I have heard most appreciative words with reference to these exhibitions uttered by many people, but not by Liberals alone, but by many foreigners and by several hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I remember that the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) spoke in most glowing terms of the use to Canada of these foreign exhibitions.
I would like the minister to make a distinction. This is not a foreign exhibition, but a festival of empire. How many have been held, and what beneficial result has come from them?

The work we propose doing there is exactly the same as that in connection with the Franco-British exhibition three years ago in London, the exhibition in Brussels last year, Milan a few years ago, and Dublin a few years before that. The work will be exactly the same. The festival of empire includes an exhibition from all the different parts of the empire, the wonderful resources, progress and industries of the empire. It is true that in addition to that there is this pageant that I spoke of. My hon. friend seems to think that is something in the nature of a circus. I do not know whether he saw the pageant at the Quebec Tercentenary, or if he is familiar with the work of Mr. Frank Lascelles the originator of these pageants whose reputation is world-wide. A pageant of this character is as far removed from the ordinary wandering show as the work of a great artist from that of an ordinary person, who knows nothing about such things. This will foe an exhibition of the marvellous history of this empire and an incitement to the people of to-day to remember and to honour the achievements of their forefathers as represented in a most magnificent way, not by a lot of hirelings but by volunteers, many of them from the best families in the Mr. SPROTJLE.
empire. I have had letters from people in Canada asking the privilege of taking part in the pageant at the Crystal Palace. Last year there were many applications when the question was first brought forward for the privilege of taking part in it, and I am informed that, as a matter of fact, there are some volunteers taking part in that pageant who are going to the expense of supplying their own dresses and everything connected with their appearance as well as spending their time in going there without our hiring or engaging a single individual. That was the case at the Tercentenary celebration at Quebec. I think I am within the mark when I say that there was not a hireling who appeared in that celebration at all ; so that my hon. friend in that respect is entirely wrong in his estimate of what is going to occur. He asks if this pageant is a festival or an exhibition. It is both combined in one, and it is to be upon the grounds of. the Crystal Palace which is one of the best resorts in the neighbourhood of London ; celebrated the world over as a place of resort for people who wish to enjoy and instruct themselves and where we will have an opportunity of making a representation of the great historical events of our empire and will at the same time be able to present the fruits of the labours, industry, progress and enterprise of the to-day people of the empire. This is an opportunity that I do not think the people of Canada would like Canada to omit being present at, and I think we would be derelict in our duty if we did not see that Canada took advantage of it. Above all my hon. friend who has a high opinion of the value of our position in the empire, and of our connection without it-
Who will represent Canada? Will my hon. friend tell me if he is going over next summer himself?

I do not think I shall, as a matter of fact. But it is a matter of no consequence because I will not appear in the pageant. I would not appear particularly in any capacity if I did go over. The people who will represent Canada in the pageant will foe the people who volunteer to do so. My hon. friend may if he chooses, and I have no doubt that they will be very happy to put him in. Those who will represent Canada in the exhibition will be the exhibition staff and they will be so busy with their work that they will not have time to take part in the pageant. As for this not being an unforseen expense ; the pageant of empire was intended to have taken place last year and a vote was taken, but in consequence of the death of the King it was postponed, and the idea being renewed when parliament prorogued we had to decide whether we would take part in it or not without consulting parliament, be-

cause had we waited for parliament it would toe too late to make the necessary preparations.
When was the money voted ?
Last session.
That would not lapse before the end of this year.

The proposed pageant last year was to be a comparatively very small affair and although the King expressed his approval it was not under his patronage. On this occasion, in view of the coronation and the colonial conference the scope of the coming pageant has been enormously increased and the vote of last year would nowhere nearly meet the necessary expenditure. We took $5,000 or $6,000 last year and spent $3,000, while now I am asking for $100,000 and I expect that the total cost will be between $250,000 and $300,000. Last year- the intention was to have Canada have a little court in the Crystal Palace building, hut this year we intend to erect a great building on the grounds and to show our products as we have been in the habit of doing at great international exhibitions. I venture to say that never before has there been a better opportunity for advertising to the people of the world, and es-peciallv to our fellow subjects of the 'empire, the glories and the greatness and the progress of Canada.

The minister stated he would be glad if my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) would volunteer for the festival of empire. What class would he 'put him in? I hope not amongst the mules, because he is a chronic kicker from the minister's standpoint.
I do not believe there will be any western bronchos in it.

If the minister does not send my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) there, he will be missing the best Canada produces. I notice amongst the expenditures for this festival of empire last year a charge of $40 for a map made by Joseph Aube, Ottawa, and $1.50 for a book, The Cradle of New France, written by A. G. Doughty. What is the explanation?
I think the map was a map of Canada, and the book is a well known book by Dr. A. G. Doughty the Dominion archivist.
How will you select the products of Canada for exhibition purposes?
The staff buys them as best they can.

What do they consist of?
',fr. FISHER. Everything we can find in Canada. We have a permanent exhibit of
minerals which we are adding to all the time, and which was one of the most magnificent exhibits at Brussels last summer. We have a timber exhibit, agricultural exhibits, fruit exhibits, fish and animal exhibits.

Does the minister think that an expenditure for an exhibition of the agricultural products of Canada will be necessary in England, if we are to secure the American market for all our Canadian produce?
I have no doubt there will be an immense number of Americans at that exhibition, and they will be able to come and buy.
Will our old friend William Hutchison be the commissioner?
Yes.

I am somewhat surprised to see how Mr. Hutchison figures in the Auditor General's Report, and it will be of great interest to the farmers of Canada to see how their money is being wasted :n that direction. William Hutchison was commissioner at the Brussels exhibition at a salary of $250 per month for one part of the term and $375 per month for the other part. In addition he got a living allowance for 144 days at $12 a day, and in addition his fare and transportation and sundry expenses and cab hire and everything else was paid by the people of Canada. Mr. Hutchison was also at the Alaskan Yukon Pacific exhibition, and there he got a salary of $250 a month and a living allowance of $20 a day for 214 days in addition to his travelling expenses, cost of sleepers, transfers, and everything else. That is a most ridiculous allowance to give to an official who is paid a salary of $250 a month. I notice that for his services at the Pacific Yukon exhibition he was paid up to the 31st of -Qetober, 1909, and on the 1st of November his salary commenced at the Brussels exhibition at $250 a month and just a week later, certainly before he had time to get to Brussels from Seattle his salary was raised to $375 per month. I would like the minister to explain how he juggled in order to get our friend William Hutchison from Seattle to Brussels inside of a week.

The exhibition branch and its work go on all the year around. It is true, when one exhibition closes another may not be officially opened for a few months; but the work of the commissioner and of his staff is just as arduous outside of exhibition times as in exhibition times -in fact, more so, for at such times they have to take down, pack and unpack all their exhibits, and see to their shipment. As a matter of fact, I know that Mr. COMMONS
Hutchison hurried from Seattle, spent only-two or three days here to talk over matters, and had only a few days in Brussels to get ready for the opening of the exhibition there. I am glad to know that he was so successful that the Canadian pavilion was the only one ready on the day of the official opening. My hon. friend speaks of Mr. Hutchison's pay. I can only say that he is inadequately paid for the service he has done for the Dominion of Canada. Mr. Hutchison seems to have a perfect genius for exhibition work. He has been permanent exhibition commissioner for Canada for over eleven years, and has attended eleven international exhibitions, and he has been honoured for the work he has done by the authorities of most of these exhibitions. He has been praised, and his work has been copied by commissioners from other countries. I had an evidence of that last spring in Brussels, where I spent a few days just after the opening of the exhibition. I met a number of the foreign commissioners. I met; also, the members of the English commission, one and all of them praised without stint the work of the Canadian commissioner and the results of his work in exhibiting Canadian products, telling me that they had derived the greatest assistance possible in Tegard to showing their own products from the advice which Mr. Hutchison had been able to give them. With regard to Mr. Hutchison's pay, I would say that for a number of years we paid him at the rate of $3,000 a year, and during the exhibition time we made him an allowance of $20 a day. This sounds a little high, but any one who knows exhibition w.orik knows that there is hardly a dav during the exhibition when he does not have visitors whom he has to entertain more or less.
That is to cover his wine account?
It is to cover all his expenses.
Surely my hon. friend does not approve of a wine account?

It includes whatever Mr. Hutchison has to get to entertain his guests. Mr. Hutchison, however, felt a little hurt at some criticisms which were made in the House last year, or the year before, and he asked me to reduce his allowance. I increased his salary, but decreased his allowance, with the result that he got several hundred dollars a yeaT less than he had been getting before. I did that at his own request, not to save the country any money, and not to make any change from my own point of view, as I did not think that Mr. Hutchison was getting too much for the services he was rendering, or the expenses to which he was put.

I desire to express my appreciation of Mr. Hutchison's services to Canada. I "have had the pleasure of attending some of the exhibitions under his management, and I have found him most courteous, obliging and painstaking towards Canadian visitors. I have had more than one experience of that kind. I believe Mr. Hutchison is a most efficient officer, and I do not believe he is overpaid. I think Canada may well be proud of Mr. Hutchison as her head official at these exhibitions. Any Canadian who visits them, whoever he may be, will receive from him most gentlemanly and courteous treatment.

I am not by any means finding fault with the amount paid to Mr. Hutchison. I am finding fault with the method of bookkeeping. I do not think it is right that the onus of spending $20 a day of the people's money should be laid upon a public servant. If he is not paid properly, I think it is up to the department to give him an adeauate recompense' for the work he is doing. To the average farmer $20 a day for spending money appears to be a very large amount. Twenty cents a day, in my country, is considered a fair amount.
Oh, no.

What amuses me is the hen. minister's description of his employees. Whether a man is a horticulturist, a botanist, an exhibition commissioner, or anything else, he is the one man par excellence for that particular job. You would imagine they were all heaven-born and government appointed.
No, Canadian-born.

The hon. minister describes every selection he has made in the superlative degree. Every one of his officials seems to have combined within him all the excellencies that it is possible to combine within the same amount of human hide. Each one seems to have been born for his particular position, whether to manage a festival of empire, an exhibition, a piggery, or a chicken hatchery. I am glad to know that they are all such excellent men, but the results, I am afraid, do not always prove it. When you pay four men $5,000 a year foT looking after a few poultry, and get a return of only a few hundred dollars, there is something wrong either with the man or with the hens. I notice that all these things are very much like the widow's cruse of oil, or the expenditure on the Transcontinental railway: they look small at first, but they seem to grow as time goes on. We are never given, at the beginning, any approximate idea of what the whole expenditure is going to be. I think it would be well, when these matters

are submitted to parliament, that we should be given some approximate idea of what they are going to cost, and what we are likely to receive in return, before we commit ourselves to an expenditure, the end of which we do not know. I am not saying anything about Mr. Hutchison; I have not attended any of the exhibitions at which he was Canadian commissioner. He may be the best man in the world fox that position, or he may be a commonplace man. Eleven years ago Mr. Hutchison was employed for one exhibition, but the department have been able to keep him engaged at other exhibitions each succeeding year up to the present. We are always told that the expense of these exhibiting at these exhibitions will be slight, and the results will be something wonderful, but as time goes on they do not pan out exactly as they were represented to us.

I have to take exception to my hon. friend's statement. I said a year and a half ago when the Brussels exhibition was started that it would cost between $125,000 and $150,000. It is costing between $125,000 and $130,000, I said this afternoon that the Festival of Empire would cost at least $250,000. I venture to say it will not cost more than $275,000.
When the minister got the first appropriation he represented that it was a comparatively small affair and would not be very expensive.

I have explained repeatedly the reason for the change, which is not only justifiable but necessary. I think it will be money well expended and my hon. friends and gentlemen with him would be amongst the first to criticise the government if they did not take part in the Festival.
Oh, no, I will exonerate the minister.
Will the agricultural exhibits be similar to those at the Alaska-Yukon exhibition.	'
To a great extent.
Is it intended to send many back-benchers supporting the government over to these exhibitions?
We never send members of parliament to exhibitions.
I see in the accounts of last year eight cases of dummies at $8.64. I was wondering if these would be supporters of the government.
We do not have any dummies on this side. Silence is sometimes golden.

I had the pleasure of attending the Brussels exhibition and I was
surprised when I heard the statement of the salary paid to Col. Hutchison, $300 a month. I do not believe he is sufficiently paid for the work he is doing. The $20 a day, I understand, is for entertaining.
At Brussels he was getting only $12 a day. .

It was not enough. I want to be fair. I believe that Mr. Hutchison is doing good work and the Canadian exhibit was a credit to him. I think there should be a fair allowance made to any man occupying such a position, and the country would be well advised in paying him a reasonable salary. I do not consider $300 or $400 a month is a fair salary for the work he is accomplishing; I would be willing to see him get $500 a month. Something should be done so that we would know exactly what was being spent in connection with the work. The minister might fix a salary which would include all other expenditures. I spent two days at the exhibition and received from Col. Hutchison all the courtesy that any one could expect. He was very kind in showing me around the exhibition and he extended to me the courtesy which he would extend to any man who went to that exhibition.

I do not agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. Col. Hutchison, in addition to his salary, gets $20 a day, so he is drawing about $10,000 a year for salary and expenses. He is getting more than the minister presiding over his department. He must be worth more than the minister himself.
Possibly he is.
Then he should take your position and you should take his, because the best man should be Minister of Agriculture.
A man may be a first-class commissioner and not be able to do something else. Col. Hutchison is commissioner for exhibitions, and he is unexcelled.
When he went to the old country he had never been in charge of an exhibition.
He had been in charge of the Central Canada Exhibition for years.
Running a small fair is nothing compared with running these exhibitions. There is no doubt the position was given to Mr. Hutchison because he was a defeated member of this House.

There is every doubt and that is not the fact. I had the appointing of Mr. Hutchison, and he was appointed to go to Buffalo because he has had experience in exhibition work and had been

the manager of the Central Canada exhibition for years and had brought it up from being a very small and unimportant exhibition to be a very good one; it was that which attracted my attention to him. He was not a defeated candidate because he did not run and was not defeated; but his having been in the House before had nothing whatever to do with his appointment.
The running of a small exhibition in Ottawa does not seem to me to. be any great qualification for the position of manager of these large exhibitions.
His success shows that it was.
The minister could have got men who had had experience'

Not so good as Col. Hutchison.
Mr. REID (Grenville) He could have got them for $10,000 a year to pay their expenses and entertain more than Col. Hutchison does. As to Col. Hutchison being a defeated candidate, I may have been wrong in that statement, but at the same time he was willing and did try to get the convention in Ottawa and could not.
Again my hon. friend was wrong because he refused to go before the convention.
Because he knew he could not win. The minister knows that his being in Ottawa and a former member of the House supporting the government was the reason for his appointment.
That is not the reason he got the appointment.
The minister can have his opinion; I have mine.
I know, but my hon. friend does not know.

No doubt, these exhibitions have done good. But what has the minister done for the farmer ? Take, for instance, the farmers of eastern Ontario, in which district I live, the minister has an experimental farm here at Ottawa, but no person sees "it, except a few who go out on excursions; no information is sent throughout the country, as to what is going on there. I have tried, and I cannot find any way in which the minister is helping the farmers of eastern Ontario. He tells us: See the way dairying in eastern Ontario has improved. Why, that is the work of the local government, which sends its instructors and inspectors to the cheese factories and creameries. The minister does not spend as much in a year in promoting the interests of the farmers as does the Depart-Mr. FISHER.
meat of Agriculture of the single province of Ontario. It is true, about a million is spent every year through the minister's department, but it goes for quarantine, for exhibitions and other things .that do not help the farmer. It seems to me the minister has lost his influence in the cabinet. When this government took office, the expenditure of the Militia Department and the Agriculture Department were about equal; now, the Minister of Militia gets appropriations of about $15 for every $1 that the Minister of Agriculture gets for agriculture. Which of these, then, has influence in the government P The Minister of Militia, of course.
Of course, he has.

Then, it is time that the farmers should demand that a man should be put iat the head of this department, who will have influence and use it in the interest of agriculture. The first thing the minister (Mr. Fisher), knows, the Minister of Labour will be getting larger appropriations for the Labour Department than he gets for the Agriculture Department. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bro-deur), smiles because since he came in, he has been able to grab more for his department, than the Minister of Agriculture, by ten to one. There is no. department that has stood still so long as that of the Minister of Agriculture, and I want the farmers from the Atlantic to .the Pacific to realize that. The minister gets a little more money for exhibitions and to pay men like Colonel Hutchison and other supporters of the government, money spent where the Public Accounts Committee cannot show up the graft that goes on because the people are on the other side of the Atlantic. So far as eastern Ontario is concerned, the minister has not done anything for the farmers for ten years. There are many ways in which he could help them, instead of lying idle.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid, Grenville), wants the . farmers to know about these things. I am afraid he will have to bring further proof than his assertions about them.

If the minister will refer to page D-12 of the Auditor General's Report, for 1909-10, under the heading Alaska-Yukon exhibition, he will find this item:
Fournier, Fournier Limited, St. Hyacinthe, P.Q.; Red Line Cocktails, 7 cases at $8, $56.
I desire an explanation of this item. Were these for the minister's own use, or were they for Mr. Hutchison to distribute among his friends ? Why these should be bought at St. Hyacinthe and exported to the Pacific coast, I do not understand, unless

it was, that the minister wanted to have really choice stuff for his own use.

I am afraid I cannot answer that question, I did not use the cocktails, and did not know they were there. Why cocktails should have been bought at St. Hyacinthe, I do not know; I was not aware that it was a particularly favoured locality in that respect. I am afraid I am not a judge of cocktails myself.
But the minister bought 7 cases at $8 a case.
I am informed that this was an exhibit, bought and sent to the Alaska-Yukon exhibition, to show what the province of Quebec could produce in these things.

I understand that these were goods bought in St. Hyacinthe for exhibition somewhere. They were bought for that purpose, because they were good goods; that is all. It is a compliment for the establishment for which I thank the hon. gentleman.

These supplementary estimates, I believe, are what they are called. The item before us is for something that has been overlooked in the original estimates. There has been an oversight in connection with a certain other exhibition. I refer to the Selkirk Centennial. The minister (Mr. Fisher), will, no doubt, thank me for calling his attention to it. Over a year ago, a delegation of important business men from Winnipeg, came here during the sitting of the House, and I believe the Minister of Agriculture received that delegation, and there were with him the Prime Minister and some other members of the government. The delegates explained their resources and put their case before the government. And I believe that the Prime Minister told them that they had not resources enough, that they must dig up some more money, and when they had done so, he would see them again. They went back. They say that they complied with his requisition, and carried out his suggestion to the letter. Since that, they have had, I believe, two or three interviews with the government, and I think the minister (Mr. Fisher), himself knows the situation. We have had some statements from the press and from some of the delegations; whether they were authorized to make those statements or not, I do not know. But the people would hear with interest the position in which the matter now stands, and they would be very much pleased, I know, to see in subsequent estimates a substantial sum to carry out that exhibition.

My hon. friend (Mr. Hag-gart, Winnipeg), understands that these j supplementary estimates are for the cur- ' 120
rent year, but the exhibition of which he speaks, is for the future. I think my hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), has stated to the House that the matter was one which was still under advisement and the government were not prepared yet to give a definite answer. I cannot say more at this time.

As to these being estimates of the current year, I might remind the minister that, this being a world's exhibition, those concerned cannot wait until that year; they must have at least three years for preparation.

Do I understand from the minister^ (Mr. Fisher) that he is going to use his influence, whatever little help it may be, towards getting the necessary money to carry on that exhibition, or bring it about? I believe that if the Minister of Agriculture would get at his fellow members in the cabinet and work a little more diligently, he would be able to accomplish something. But since I came here I have observed that the Minister of Agriculture does not ring in and try to get the money that is due to the agriculturists of this country, in order that they may show to the world at large what Canada can do in that line. There is no doubt that our agriculturists have the greatest claim for government assistance of any class or profession in Canada, but judging from the figures in the estimates year after year, they are not getting their just portion of the expenditure. I am not criticising what- other departments may spend, but I am criticising that minister for not expending on agriculture what we are entitled to. The farmers pay the greatest portion of the taxation, as is well known, and that is a consideration that should have more weight with the government than it appears to have. It is all right to put the blame on the Prime Minister. But this world's fair at Winnipeg is practically an agricultural undertaking. There is no doubt that it would do more for that western country in showing the world what it is capable of, and what all Canada is capable of, than anything else the minister could think of. But unless he rings in his fellow-members and tells them that he is going to give the agriculturists what they are entitled to, I do not see much hope of his succeeding. Now, I want the minister to make a promise that he will do his utmost towards getting such an appropriation for the Winnipeg centennial, as the delegates from that city have asked for, in order that they may proceed with the great _ undertaking. If the minister will promise to use his efforts with his colleagues, perhaps he will be able to accomplish something.

The hon. gentleman does not encourage me to do that, because he



379&
says I have no influence, and that I do not succeed with my colleagues.
I want you to rehabilitate yourself.

I can only say that I have no doubt whatever that an expenditure of this kind on a world's exhibition in Winnipeg, or at some other central place in Canada, in the near future, would do this country a great deal of good.
Does not the minister think that Winnipeg is the best place?

I am not sure, but I am inclined to think that Winnipeg would be the best place for such an exhibition, and I have no doubt that Canada could make such a display there as would attract a great deal of attention throughout the world.

It is not my intention to find any fault with this amount, but I want to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that the agriculturists of Canada are getting this year less than one million dollars from the government, and even one-tenth of that is going to this festival in England. I am not saying that is wrong, but I do say that it is a disgrace to Canada that less than one million dollars is expended for the benefit of this, the greatest industry in Canada. I do not think the farmers have a right to more than their share, nor do I think that they have been asking too much, but no man can honestly stand up in this House and say that the farmers are asking too much, when the fact is that less than one million dollars are expended on the agricultural industry, on the other hand. Now, I believe that if the minister tried to do his duty he could get more for this industry than he has been getting. It was a common saying among the farmers' delegation which came to Ottawa from the west, that this Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa was a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada.
I heard many people say just the reverse.

I want to tell the minister, from a farmer's, standpoint, that if the people in the county I represent could not produce better stock than he has on that farm, I would be ashamed of them. That is a fact, and I am not trying to make little of the farm, either. But I can honestly tell the minister that farmer after farmer that goes to that agricultural college says that it is a disgrace to this Dominion. I have seen for myself, as hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House have seen, and know well, that there are pigs kept there, I suppose for breeding purposes, who were born blind, and they are kept there as a disgrace to this Do-Mr. FISHER.
minion. Now, the minister says that some people tell him that the dairy was well kept there. Now, the minister's, own report of 1910 shows that the milk products of his dairy herd only amounted to 6,115-pounds. Now, there are herds in this Dominion that produce over 10,000 pounds. _ I say that this experimental farm, which-should be the greatest and the best kept in the Dominion, makes a very poor showing, after it has been in existence for a quarter of a century, and still has a dairy herd the production of which is only a little more than half that of other herds in this Dominion. Now, I say that these are facts that cannot be got over. I find them in the minister's own report. I do not think it becomes a country such as Canada to occupy that position. I have been at that experimental farm myself twice during the last session, and once this session, and I say that the beef cattle there-I presume they are beef cattle, we know that there are only two purposes for which cattle are kept, one for dairy and the other for beef-and the beef cattle at the experimental farm, with the exception of a few that were imported, are a disgrace to any farm, let alone the experimental farm.
Does my hon. friend refer to the shorthorn herds there?

These experimental farms ought to ibe located in different parts of the four provinces of the west, because there we have a very big territory and an experiment that will prove useful in one locality is not applicable three or four hundred miles away under different climatic conditions, and different quality of soil. Anything the minister can do in the direction of improving agriculture in the west will have my ardent support, but when it comes to wasting money in this way I must object to it.

As has been pointed out by my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) not more than $383,000 of this large vote is actually expended in the interests of the farmers of Canada. That alone proves that the Minister of Agriculture is not devoting himself as he ought to the improvement and advancement of agriculture in this country. This government has now $130,000,000 a year to spend, and yet the Minister of Agriculture has not, since they came to .power, been able to get the Minister of Finance to spend one dollar more in the interests of the farmers than was expended by the 'Conservative government when the annual revenue was only one-third of what it is to-day. It seems strange that the Minister of Militia can influence the Minister of Finance to give him ten dollars for every one dollar he gives to the Minister of Agriculture.

The hon. gentleman from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) has referred to the establishment of experimental farms, and when the item for that purpose comes before the House I think he will see that I am meeting his views in that respect to a large extent. I regard this as a very important expenditure, and I am sure that it will receive fair consideration from this side of the House. I accept all the responsibility for that.
Does he think that the expenditure for agriculture is sufficient or fair, compared with the expenditure on the militia of Canada ?

I am not going to criticise the expenditures of other departments. I have been able to obtain for agriculture all the money I have asked for.
