Technical Education Commission-further amount required, $10,000.

This amount is required to enable the Commission on Technical Education to continue during the balance of tire present fiscal year the work which it is now carrying on. At the last session of parliament $25,000 was voted towards the expenses of this commission. The commission has now been engaged for about seven months, and the appropriation made by parliament last year has been exhausted.
Will the minister explain bow the money already voted has been expended ?

The commission entered upon its duties about the 18th of July last, and it has held sittings in the different cities and towns of the Dominion, has visited industrial establishments and taken evidence under oath, from manufacturers, workingmen and educationalists as to the needs of -the Dominion in the matter of industrial training and technical education. Up to the present time, the commission has visited 99 -different localities, and has heard 1,466 witnesses. It commenced its work at the Atlantic coast and has followed a course which ha-s taken it through the different provinces to -the Pacific. The work oi taking evidence in Canada will be completed with the session to be held in _ Ottawa next week, and then the commission will prepare an interim report summing up the findings so far as the needs of the Dominion are concerned. It will then go abroad and study the methods adopted in other countries to meet similiar, needs. The members of the commission have travelled about 10,000 miles.
What is expected to be the total cost of this commission ?

$25,000 has already been voted, $25,000 will be asked in the estimates for next year, and $10,000 is asked
in this vote. I should think this would be enough to enable the commission to complete its inquiries. Something further may be necessary for the publication of the report.
When is it expected to be completed ?
It is expected that the commission will return from abroad in the latter part of August, and I hope to have the report ready for presentation to parliament in -the session to be held next fall.
Do the commissioners travel together ?

In the larger centres, like Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, they have sat together, but in some cases they have divided, and two or three have visited one locality and two or three another.
Was there any special reason for having such a large commission ?

The reasons that governed the number of the commission were that the subject was a large one, and the Dominion a large dominion, and a great many interests had to be considered. The manufacturers had made strong representations as to the need of this commission, and it was thought well to have -a representative of them. Similarly the labour men had made strong representations, and it was thought advisable to have them represented. The commission does not seem to be too large, considering the nature of its work.
Will agriculture be taken up at all?

Yes; agriculture is one of the subjects, and my hon. friend will recognize in the name of Dr. Robertson, who is chairman of the commission, one of the leading agricultural authorities in the Dominion. With Dr. Robertson on the commission as chairman, I think the hon. member may feel quite sure that the agricultural interests will be very fully inquired into.
On whose recommendation was the manufacturers' representative selected?

The manufacturers presented their veiws to the government on the subject through Mr. Murray, secretary of the Manufacturers' Association, who had made a very complete study, up to a certain point of the subject from the manufacturers' point of view. The government felt that they could not give greater satisfaction to the manufacturers than if they chose for the commission the man whom the manu-

facturers had themselves chosen to present to the government the needs of such a commission. That is why Mr. Murray was chosen.
I understand that some of the provincial legislatures are also inquiring into this question. Is there any cooperation between this government, and, say, the government of Ontario?

Yes; I am happy to say there has been the most cordial co-operation. In each instance the members of the commission, in visiting ia province,. have called first of all upon the Prime Minister and members of the government of the province being visited and explained that the federal government, before appointing the commission, had conferred with the premiers of the several provinces, and had secured from them their express wish that the federal government should take this step and co-operate with the provinces. In each case the provincial government, Dr. Robertson informs me, has done everything in its power to assist the federal commission in getting information. In Toronto, for instance, Sir James Whitney's government had appointed Mr. Seath a commissioner to inquire into certain phases of the work. Mr. Seath intimated to the chairman of the commission that he had been instructed by his government to give to the federal government's commission the benefit of his views in advance of submitting his report to his own government, should [DOT]this be desired, he of course intimated that he would prefer giving his report to his own government. I mention that to show the hearty manner in which the provincial authorities have co-operated. Prof. Robertson assures me that in every province the provincial authorities have expedited the work of the commission and have used their good offices to see that the commission got the fullest information possible.
What salaries do the commissioners receive?

Each commissioner receives $16 a day and his necessary travelling expenses. Out of the $16 the members of the commission pay their own hotel and incidental expenses, and they do not receive any remuneration for Sundays.
How was the labour representative elected

In a manner similar to the selection of the representative of the manufacturing interests. The Trades and Labour Congress, for a number of years past, have been asking the government to appoint this commission and on each occasion they have designated Mr. Simpson, the vicepresident of the Trades and Labour Council, to present their case to the government, and, in fact, the Dominion Trades and Mr. KING.
Labour Congress at one conference suggested that Mr. Simpson should be the person appointed to represent labour in the event of the request being granted, so the government simply took the nominee of the Trades and Labour Congress.
What is Mr. Simpson's occupation?

A reporter, I think, on the Toronto * Star.' He seems to be especially well qualified for this position. He was a former vice-president of the Trades and Labour Congress, and was, as I have mentioned, nominated by that body as their representative. He was, at the time of his appointment, chairman of the Toronto Board of Education. He had been a member of a special committee on technical education of the Toronto board in 1906. He was a member of the Technical Education Commission which visited seven United States cities and recommended a curriculum for the new Toronto Technical School in 1909. He had presented the subject of technical education before the provincial government at different times.
Was he a candidate for parliamentary honours?
No; I do not think so. I might say that so far as I know he is not a Liberal.
Are the members all the same?
I cannot say what the politics of some of them are. The government sought to choose the best men.

I presume it would be one of the duties of the commission to outline a scheme by which technical schools may be established and maintained jointly with the provinces or independently of the provinces, and to suggest the curriculum of study.
Mr. IylNG. Yes; the commission is for the purpose of gathering information generally which will be compiled in the form of a report, and this report will then be available for distribution, and the provinces may take on this report such action as they think best. The scope of the commission would be best indicated by this communication, which the chairman of the commission lias sent out in each locality visited. In each case it has been similar to the following.
Royal Commission on Industrial Training and Technical Education.
Ottawa, Ont., December 27, 1910.
Dear Sir,-I have the honour to intimate to you that the Royal Commission on Industrial Training and Technical Education proposes to visit places according to the itinerary outlined in the sheet which is inclosed herewith.
The commission will give particular at-

tention to the manufacturing industries, to agriculture, to domestic occupations, to mining, to the fisheries, to the lumber interests, to the building trades, to the transportation services, as well as to the technical training required for commercial operations.
The commission will also make inquiry into, (a) the needs of existing industries in respect of labour, (b) the quality of labour which is available, and (c) the needs of such labour for industrial training and technical education.
The plan for the work of the commission at each place has ordinarily been as follows::- A local committee representing the mayor, the board of trade, the manufacturers" association, the educational institutions, the trades and labour interests, and any organization identified with training for women, makes provision for a place in which to hold the sessions of the commission. That is usually the council chamber or court house. The local committee also notifies persons who represent the various local interests and industries that they will be expected to appear before the commission to testify in regard to the present equipment and needs of the place and locality in respect to industrial training and technical education. The commission devotes part of each day to visiting the industrial establishments and educational institutions, and holds one or two sessions to receive testimony from those who desire to appear before it. The inquiry is ordinarily conducted by questions and answers, although those who appear before the commission may present information either by oral or written statement, bearing on the matters of the inquiry.
The commission will appreciate your cooperation in any manner which you may consider appropriate regarding any or all of these matters.
A reply to this might be addressed, care of Deputy Minister of Labour, Ottawa.
I have the honour to be. Sir,
Your most obedient servant.

Partly and partly not. What I had in mind was this: there are many people in the country who desire to acquire knowledge of the principles of certain arts ox trades, nut with a view to making them a permanent lifework. but with a view to equipping themselves better for that which they have chosen as their lifework. For instance, many a young man would like to gain knowledge with Tegard to mechanics, another with regard to agriculture. Will there be in these technical schools, branches where agriculture, mechanics, artisan's work, and other lines will be taught ?

It is impossible for me to anticipate what the recommendations of the commission will he, but the scope of the commission, as I understand it, covers just the kind of thing my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), has suggested. I asked Dr.
Robertson if he would give me a brief statement of what, up to the present, had come under the notice of the commission along the lines they were likely to report upon. Perhaps, if I read his statement, .that will indicate to what extent the commission has in mind, making recommendation along the line my hon. friend has spoken of. This is Dr. Robertson's statement:
In general the testimony has been that provision for industrial training and technical education, in institutions and industrial establishments, exists in very few places and in them not to an extent adequate to the needs of the industrial population. The testimony indicates that some further opportunities are necessary to enable young men and women, from the ages of 14 to 18, to enter upon the various industrial and productive occupations with such educational qualifications that they may become industrially efficient.
I.	In almost every place representative men
have stated that urgent need exists for night classes for boys, after the age of 14, who have left the day schools.	_
II.	The workmen have been practically unanimous in the expression of a desire for opportunities for such a measure of technical education as will enable them to acquire a knowledge of the principles which underlie the processes of their occupations, and also to give the more energetic and ambitious of them a fair working chance to prepare themselves for advancement and promotion.
III.	There has been a unanimous expression of opinion that the several towns need some provision for industrial training and technical education which, in its general character, shall have an educational value equivalent to the high school or academy courses of study, but which shall be adapted specifically and directly to the needs of those who are to enter upon industrial occupations: and also to meet the case of those who wonld like to matriculate into, or enter upon the more advanced work of, technical colleges or agricultural colleges.
IV.	Statements in respect of these four matters have come alike from the representatives of industries, from those who are responsible for educational work, and from the workingmen and women themselves. Not only are they all agreed as to the need for industrial training and technical education, but they have evinced enthusiastic keenness in offering co-operation, towards meeting the need in some adequate manner.
In other words, the .commission has been endeavouring to ascertain from as many sources as possible, wbat are the needs in Canada, with respect to the different industries and industrial callings which employers and artisans are experiencing in the matter of a proper equipment for industrial efficiency. I think they have already got a good idea of the needs of Canada. The idea now, is that they should visit Europe and see how similar needs are being met in the different countries there. They will then return and <prepare a report which will be of service in enabling the provinces of

this country to shape their educational work, so far as it relates to industrial training and technical education, along lines which will be of the greatest benefit to the classes in whose interest the work is undertaken.
Will this cover the field for female as well as male labour ?
Yes, _ That is a phase to which the commission is devoting some special attention.
Are there any females on the commission ?
No, but a number of female witnesses have testified before the commission.

It does seem to me, thinking it over, that it might have been the part of wisdom fx* have one member of the commission, at least, .an intelligent lady, who had shown an aptitude for such educational work and had acquired a general knowledge of industrial life among the female population.
I think there is much to be said in favour of that view.
If I followed the figures correctly, we have voted $25,000, and are voting $10,000 now, and I understand that $25,000 more is likely to be asked for in the
Main estimates of next year.

I answered a moment ago, that possibly the printing of the report will require some further appropriation. I am inclined to think it will take $25,000 to cover the expenses of the commission in Europe.

speechtext: It has been urged upon the department that better protection should be given to the fisheries on the British Columbia coast, and it has been considered advisable that we should charter a couple of vessels for that purpose. speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned the matter, and I will furnish him with the reason for that change. I may say that in British Columbia, the western provinces, and the maritime provinces the overseers are all appointed by the federal government; I do not think there are any other overseers in those provinces except those appointed by the federal government, though there may be a few appointed by the provincial authorities. It was found advisable that we should have in Ontario our own officers to carry out our own laws and regulations. Formerly, all the officers were appointed by the federal authorities. But by a judgment which was rendered in 1898, it was decided that the beds of the rivers above the tide were the property of the provinces, and that the provinces had some rights in the fisheries, one of which was to issue licenses for catching fish. As a result of that judgment, most of the officers were kept on by the provincial authorities; we had, however, to maintain a limited number of our own officers. It was found, however, that the provincial officers were looking chiefly after the execution of the provincial regulations concerning the issuing of licenses, they were not supposed to carry out the federal regulations. It seemed proper, therefore, that the regulations passed by the federal authorities should be carried out by federal officers. I am not making any reflection upon the way the fisheries had been protected by the provincial officers, but they were not of course appointed to carry out our regulations. There were numerous complaints that our regulations were not properly enforced, and facts were reported to the department which rendered it advisable for us to appoint our own officers to look after the protection of the fisheries in pursuance of our own regulations.

I would like to ask the minister regarding the appointment of some 37 fishery overseers in the province of Ontario-as to what their duties will be, why they are now appointed, seeing that no such officers were required before, and whether they are to take the place of the provincial overseers now discharging duties of a like character, or whether they are to implement their work by doing some other kind of work in connection with the protection of the fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
As I have already explained, since the judgment rendered by the Privy Council on the fisheries case, both the provincial and the Dominion authorities now exercise jurisdiction over the fisheries. It was decided by the Privy Council that the provinces, by virtue of their proprietary rights in the fisheries, are entitled to issue licenses and to make regulations as to the manner in which those licenses shall be issued. By the same judgment it was recognized that the regulation of the fisheries, generaly speaking, devolved upon the Dominion authorities. So that there is to-day a double jurisdiction in respect to the fisheries. The Dominion authorities are required to adopt the necessary laws and regulations for the protection and preservation of the fisheries, and we have been trying to exercise our powers according to our best judgment. We found that the regulations affecting the fisheries were not properly carried out. In Ontario there were only three officers to exercise supervision over the fisheries. The provincial officers are necessarily called upon to look after the observance of the laws and regulations passed by the provincial authorities concerning licenses. They have to see whether there are many people fishing without licenses, and, if so, to call upon them to cease fishing. But there are many regulations over which the provincial authorities have no jurisdiction, such as those relating to the size of the mesh, the gears with which fishing operations are carried on the close seasons, &c.
We had only three officers in Ontario who had general supervision. We could not expect the provincial authorities to enforce the observance of the Dominion laws and regulations. As there were complaints that our own regulations weTe not properly observed we thought of appointing a certain number of officers, whose duties *would be to look after the carrying out of
those laws and regulations. I have divided the province into districts and have appointed about 40 officers, who axe going to supervise the fisheries in Ontario, as the officers axe doing in the provinces I have mentioned. We have adopted a new principle of having a less number of officers who will be called upon to devote all their time to this work, and we expect that the salary they will receive from the government will enable them to discharge their duties in such a way that the complaints which existed before, as to the carrying out of our regulations, will not be heard in future. These officers will enforce the Dominion laws and regulations and will Teport violations of them to the Dominion authorities, and on the advice of the department, take the necessary action.
The Dominion authorities do not propose to issue licenses to fishermen to fish, that will be left in the hands of the Ontario government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The authority of the provincial government of Ontario in that respect, is absolute, we have no right to prevent them from issuing licenses. We have, however, the right ourselves, which was not denied to us by the judgment of the Privy Council, to issue licenses. We do not intend for a moment to exercise any such right.

I cannot understand why it is necessary to appoint a lot of these officers in Ontario. I assume that the minister wants to run his department as economically as possible and not to appoint unnecessary officers. Between Kingston and Brockville the Ontario government have three efficient fishery overseers. They have gasoline launches running up and down all the time to see that the laws are not violated, that nets are not used. The overseer in my county has a wagon load of nets that have been seized. Through the good work of these overseers there is now practically no illegal fishing there. It looks as if the minister is simply appointing these men to give them positions and that men will be paid as fishery overseers to do electioneering work. I defy the minister to show where these officials are going to bs of any use. At Brockville there are now two officials appointed by the Ontario government, who are doing the work properly. There were complaints a few years ago that the Ontario government officials did not do good work and the reason was, that they paid men $50 a year and of course, the men could not be expected to do work of that kind for that salary.
What do they get now ?

They now get $300 for the season and a launch. The present Ontario government, when they

came in, saw fit to pay a reasonable salary. I suppose the minister will pay about $600, but the men he -appoints, cannot do anything more than is done by the men -now on the ground. How much territory will the man at Brockville cover ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: He is to supervise the Thousand Island district from Lake Ontario down.

That would be from east of Kingston to perhaps Brockville and there are now three men in that district. In appointing these men did the minister consider that there is now an efficient staff of provincial government officials, and did he consult the Ontario government to see whether they ihad men doing the same work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We made our organization to cover Ontario with our own officers. My hon. friend says the service has been well performed by the Ontario officers. The department has no means of ascertaining such a point, for we never get any information from these men. If there have been violations, seizures and impositions of penalties, they have not been reported to us.
I take it that the minister receives the official records the Ontario government -are supposed to reports, these official records, come to him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We get their annual report, that is all. The men appointed by the Ontario government are supposed to look after the enforcement of the laws of Ontario, and not to enforce the Dominion regulations. In fact, I do not think they have authority to' do it.

In the official record of the Ontario government there is a report of every fishery overseer, and I cannot believe but that the minister or his officials see that record showdng the number of seizures and the fines imposed. If there are any laws of the Dominion which will assist in protecting the fisheries there is no doubt that the Ontario fishery overseer would use those laws in addition to the Ontario law. In making these appointments along the River St. Lawrence, the minister should have taken that into consideration. I think it does not show the best administration of the department that he has never even consulted the Ontario government on this subject. And now he has to admit to the House that he never even knew they issued an official report of the work done by the Ontario fisheries service. The appointment by the minister of a lot of officials under these conditions is simply squandering the people's money.1

As I spend, whenever I can, a month or more in Muskoka-where there used to be plenty of fishing, and still is some-I know a little on this subject. The Ontario government, for some years past, has been making very strenuous efforts to do something practical in the way of protecting the fisheries. They have, at the head of the department there, an old sportsman, Mr. Tinsley, a very strong and very good Liberal, appointed by the Conservative government of Ontario, to supervise this work. He is a most excellent man and was appointed simply because of his lifelong experience. On these lakes the Ontario government has officers who supervise everything connected with the fisheries from the point of view of the provincial law. What I fear from what I have seen of the minister's proposal is that we shall come to a realization of the old proverb, that too many cooks spoil the broth. With two governments, Dominion and provincial, acting independently and without communication, neither knowing what the other is doing, you will find the Dominion officers and Ontario officers getting into what is called a ' scrap ' occasionally. Besides, you will find that when alleged violators of the law are summoned before the magistrate by the officers of one government, they will plead that they were acting in accordance with what was told them by the officer of the other government. So, between the two, we shall have no law, or worse than no law. In the interests of us all, not only those who live by fishing, but those who take pleasure in fishing, the fishery laws should be enforced. Both governments are striving for the same end. But the present method is very much as though you had two officers in the same custom house, each entitled to exercise his own judgment as to the duties to be charged upon goods. You cannot have effective work under such a method. I would beg the minister (M-r. Brodeur) to consider whether he should not send the chief officer of his department to meet the chief fishery officers of Ontario and Quebec, or ask the provincial officers to come here and discuss the possibility of agreeing upon a common system. If you act independently my judgment is you will ruin every-, thing.

In justice to the overseer in my county, because there is a very important fishing station adjacent to the county of Halton, I -want to say that I have no recollection of hearing any complaints such as the minister speaks of in respect to the non-enforcement of the regulations. I am quite sure that the Ontario overseer there insists stringently upon the regulations being observed, the chief one of which has reference to the size -of the

mesh, the other I suppose would be the close season. But I have not heard any complaints with regard to neglect of duty or of the non-observance of the regulations. The fishery overseer there considers it his duty to see that the regulations of this government are enforced as regards the size of the mesh, and the close season.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has raised this important question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the provincial authorities with regard to the fisheries. I may remark that before 1898 the fisheries were entirely administered by the federal authorities. Since then, as a result of a legal decision, the jurisdiction has been divided ; that is to say, everything pertaining to the issuing of licenses was taken over by the provincial authorities. Although the Dominion authorities had power to issue certain licenses, we have not- exercised that power, but have left it entirely in the hands of the provincial authorities. However, I -agree with my hon. friend that this dual jurisdiction is not at all satisfactory. I hope that some day the two authorities will be able to reach a settlement of this question of jurisdiction. I may say to my hon. friend that I have discussed the matter -with a minister of the provincial government, and I think we are not very far apart. I think in view of the good relations which exist to-day between the two authorities as to the administration of the fisheries of Ontario, we may be able before long to reach a compromise, or a settlement, -which will put an end to this dual jurisdiction. But it would be premature to discuss that question now in the House. It may be a question whether the fisheries should not be administered entirely by the Dominion authorities, and that we should pay a certain amount of money to the provincial authorities in lieu of the licenses. Now there are two important features of the case to keep in mind. In .a short time we are going to have in force regulations on the Great Lakes, -and the boundary waters between the United States and Canada, that is to say, upon the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence where that river forms the international boundary, the Niagara river, the Detroit river, the St. Clair river, and the St. Mary's river. The treaty between the two countries which has been laid before the House provides that regulations shall be made 'by two commissioners, one appointed by this government and one appointed by the United States government. Those regulations have been framed and have been laid before the House, and in .a very short time, perhaps, the proclamation will be issued 'by the two governments declaring that these regulations shall govern the fisheries on the Great Lakes and
the boundary rivers. In such a case, as my hon. friend from Hamilton knows, the treaty will have to be enforced by the Dominion authorities, because there is a special provision in the British North America Act to the effect that laws which have to be passed in execution of treaties must ibe enforced by the Dominion authorities. It -will, therefore, become our duty when these regulations are passed to see that they are enforced on the lakes and rivers I have just mentioned. Perhaps we could reach a settlement on thi3 basis : That we should assume the protection of the fisheries on the Great Lakes, while the provincial authorities took over the protection of the inland fisheries and their regulations ; that of course, would require an /amendment to the British North America Act. But I think that every effort should be made to reach a settlement of some kind, because this divided jurisdiction, even with the best intentions in the world on both sides, leads to some conflict. Take the question of the fish hatcheries for example. The /hatcheries which 'exist in the province of Ontario have -all been built by this government, the Ontario government has no hatcheries.

There are private
hatcheries.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I mean the provincial government has none.
I am not so sure that the hon. gentleman is correct. They send up large quantities of fry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
There may be a few hatcheries controlled by the provincial government, but the federal government has built practically the whole of them, and maintains them. When the eggs become ripe, and /are hatched, the fry -might be considered to a certain extent as the property of the provincial authorities. Therefore, we are spending money for the artificial -propagation of fish which becomes the -property of the province, -and for which they issue licenses. Well, many people say : Why should you go on -and build more hatcheries? Why do you not make an /agreement with the provincial authorities by which at least you may [DOT] get a share of the money which comes from the licenses? Remember that all the revenue which comes out of the fisheries goes into the provincial treasury and the Dominion treasury gets nothing. This is evidently an unjust situation, -and the sooner we reach an agreement in that respect the better it will be for all parties concerned. My hon. friend spoke about the absence of relations between the officers and the department. I may say that so /far -as I am concerned, I have had several opportunities to meet one of the prin-

cipal officials of the provincial government, we have been often in communication discussing questions of general interest, both by correspondence and otherwise. Besides, the officers of the department are in constant communication with the officer whose name has been given by my hon. friend. Coming to the question of the observance of our regulations, it has been alleged that there has ibeen a violation of them. If so it cannot be wondered at. Regulations are, in the ordinary nature of things very often violated. I do not know if that is the case, but no report was made to us by the provincial authorities or their officers that there had been violations or that penalties had been imposed. The hon. member for Grenville has referred to the fact that in the report issued by the provincial government it is stated that a num-be of penalties have been imposed. We have their report, and we have noted its contents but there is nothing in the report which says that these penalties have been recovered for violations of our own regulations. They must have been violations of the provincial regulations concerning the issuing of licenses. If they had been violations of our regulations concerning gears, size of mesh, or close season they would have been reported to us.
But they do not issue any licenses at all on the St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, but generally speaking.
But you spoke of complaints in so far as the St. Lawrence is concerned. I say that they do not issue any licenses at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I speak generally of Ontario, I do not speak particularly of the St. Lawrence, because I know that they do not issue any licenses there. If there have been some violations of the close season they should have been reported to us. If penalties have been imposed and money has been collected as a result of these violations not only should the violation have been reported to us but the money itself should have been returned to us.
It has reference to the close season established by the Ontario government in the St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
No, the provincial authorities have no right to make any regulations as to close seasons. If they make regulations they are entirely ultra vires. They would be against the law because the right to regulate the fisheries belongs exclusively to this parliament. But, they have the right to issue licenses and they may make regulations in connection with the issuing of licenses. But, they would have no right to determine any close Mr. BRODEUR.
season different from the one which had been determined by this government. A similar case was brought up in one of the provinces and it was decided by the Superior Court that the province had no right to make any close season. I do not know but that the case is now before the Privy Council.

I would like to understand the situation in the St. Lawrence. The minister states that the Ontario government have no right to make any close season unless it is in connection with the issuing of licenses. I suppose that their law is the same in so far as the close season is concerned as that of the Dominion. If they established a regulation in so far as close seasons are concerned, I suppose it would apply to licenses only. Is that how I am to understand it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The Dominion parliament and the Governor in Council have the right to make regulations as to close seasons. The provincial government cannot do it.
As I understand there are regulations now of the Ontario government under which there are close seasons.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No.
I understand that on the St. Lawrence

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, let us take the season for bass for instance; the close season or the open season is determined by a regulation passed by the Dominion authorities here, whether by Act of parliament or by order in council. The right to issue permits for the catching of bass may be exercised by the provincial authorities and licenses may be issued for the open season which is provided by our own regulations.

I know that the fishery overseers appointed by the provincial government have printed instructions about the close seasons when bass and other fish cannot be caught. If the minister states that close seasons cannot be established by the Ontario government then they must be acting under the laws of the Dominion government and the Ontario government may have conveyed the instructions of the Dominion government to these overseers, by making their licenses conform with the regulations of the Dominion government. As these three overseers on the St. Lawrence are carrying out the regulations as to close seasons, as they are doing the work faithfully, constantly running up and down the river, and as no licenses are issued at all at the present time, I would like to know what there is for another man to do.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The provincial authorities may have their own officers to carry out the regulations which they have the right to make with regard to the licenses themselves. They have a right to see whether a person is fishing with or without a license or, it may be, to make some further regulation in connection with the issuing of licenses, but as to general regulations with regard to gears, close seasons, open seasons, &c., there is only one authority and it is the Dominion authority. The law says that these regulations have to be enforced by the fishery officers appointed under this Act. If these officers appointed by the Ontario government have undertaken to carry out these laws they may find that they have not the right to do it; in fact, they do not undertake to do it because they do not report to us any violations of their own regulations. Will not my hon. friend admit that in that case it is very much better that We should have our men to report to us all the information with regard to the fisheries? Should we require to change the regulations concerning the fishing season these three officers do not travel the country enough to be able to inform us as to local conditions which it is absolutely necessary we should be aware of. For instance, the size of the mesh is a very important matter and we must have men on the spot to report to us as to that and other such matters of detail.

I admit that the Minister of Marine like the provincial minister, is desirous of carrying out the law for the general good, but where we have the admitted difficulty of a dual authority surely it is the duty of the governments to see whether or not, in the public interest, they can agree upon a common ground. If the minister is going to appoint a lot of officers to see that Dominion rights are vindicated and the provinces are actuated by a similar spirit the result is that you have thrust upon the Dominion, as upon the provinces, a host of officials. In two years you find, perhaps that the people condemn the whole thing and force the Dominion and the provinces to agree upon a uniform system, and then you have to pension your officials and you are thus mortgaging the country to a considerable extent. Why should not the federal Department of Fisheries agree with the representative officers of the province upon a common mode of work. No province in this Dominion is more anxious for the preservation of the fish than the province of Ontario. They have spent large sums from year to year and they are prepared to expend still more towards that end. But if the province should know that there is a big sum of money per annum paid out by the Dominion to overlap their work, instead of good, mischief will be done. I cannot
see why in a matter of common interest the federal officials cannot sit down with the provincial officials like business men and agree upon what is right for all. You are standing apart holding each other at arms length, each insisting on its right, and that means that somebody suffers between the two. There are millions of dollars brought into Ontario every year by families who come from the United States to the Muskoka lakes, the Thousand islands and Georgian bay, and who fancy they will have some fishing. The cultivation of that business is of enormous value. On the Muskoka lakes I simoose $1,000,000 have been expended by Americans in erecting dwellings; they sit on the wharfs and if they catch one fish a day they are content, but they want to do the fishing. There is no use telling these people that they have to inquire whether it is the Hon. Mr. Bro-deur at Ottawa, or some gentleman at Toronto, who lays down the law; their only desire is to know what the law is. Surely the rights of the people are paramount to the dignity of any official whether provincial or federal. Before we sanction the payment of a host of officers and give them the powers of the czar, we should ask the minister whether any effort has been made with the provincial minister to agree upon a common system. However zealous* the federal officers may be they cannot be more zealous than the Ontario officer, a good old Liberal, a man who gives his life to the business, a sportsman who has his heart in it; and who was appointed by the Ontario Conservative government because of his qualifications. He is just as anxious to do what you want as any man could be, and why not sit down with him and agree upon common regulations. What is the sense of having one set of regulations here and another in Toronto, and two officials going to the person and fighting over the body of the prisoner to see who will get him. I submit that is not business like.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I am absolutely converted to the idea of putting an end to this dual jurisdiction, and for years past I have made many efforts to bring about the result the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) desires. As far as the maritime provinces are concerned, the matter is in very good shape. In fact, we have reached an agreement with the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. So far as Quebec is concerned, the gulf part of the province is under the exclusive control of the federal authorities, who not only make regulations concerning the way in which fishing shall be carried on, but issue licenses and maintain vessels for the protection of the fishermen and the fishing industry. In the inland part of the province, the provincial authorities issue licenses, and the regulations, so far as I have seen, are generally well enforced. In the province

of British Columbia there is the question of jurisdiction, which has been submitted for the judgment of the Supreme Court, and I expect that the matter will be reviewed during this month. Hon. gentlemen opposite have suggested that we should agree with the provincial authorities as to the question of making regulations. Less than four months ago the provincial authorities of British Columbia and ourselves agreed that we should have a regulation as to boat rating in the northern part of the province, and a commission was appointed composed of their chief officer and one of our inspectors for British Columbia. They went on the ground of the interested parties, and made a report, which I adopted, and my colleagues accepted my recommendation that this boat rating should be observed. I fully agree with my hon. friend that this overlapping of jurisdiction is not for the benefit of the fisheries themselves, but rather is very detrimental to them, and the sooner the question is settled the better. It is not a question that can be settled by the officers; it will have to be settled by the representatives of the respective governments. In regard to improving the regulations, I thought I should have the provincial minister of Ontario come and confer with me as to the regulations which should be adopted for the Great Lakes, and we passed a few days together and discussed the regulations. I mention this just to show my hon. friends that good relations exist between us. But the fact remains that there is overlapping. In some parts of Ontario we are face to face with the depletion of the fisheries, and some day, when the fisheries have disappeared, it may be charged against us that we did not protect them, if we do not now look after the regulations for that purpose. Some reference has been made to politics. There is no politics in the administration of my department in respect to the fisheries. We do not claim not to make any mistakes, but we try our best to meet the exigencies of the situation by adopting the best regulations possible to preserve the fisheries. In some provinces we are issuing licenses, and they are issued to bona fide fishermen, and I have never heard of any complaint that we are granting licenses or refusing licenses for the purpose of obtaining any party advantage.

I quite agree with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that it is very unfortunate that the jurisdiction with respect to the fisheries has, by the decision of the Privy Council, been made concurrent as between the provinces and the Dominion. But I cannot agree with him, at least so far as my section of the country is concerned, that the fishery regulations are not being enforced. Indeed, in my county the complaint made is that when the Ontario government took charge Mr. BRODEUR.
of the regulations they were made too stringent, and I know of four cases where seizures have been made for infringements of the fishery laws. In one case at least the seizure was unjustly made, and the man was returned his nets and is going to be compensated for the injury done him. I think it is unfortunate, from what has been said to-night, that the minister did not delay the appointment of these 40 overseers in Ontario, because their duties will overlap those of the provincial officers. There will be two sets of officers to punish people for the offences committed. If a man fishes within the close season, the minister contends that the provincial officers have no right to prosecute him. On the other hand, if he fishes without a license, the Dominion officer would have no right to interfere with him. How is a Dominion official to know whether a man is fishing without a license or not? He would have to get that information from a provincial officer. On the other hand, when a man is fishing in the spring of the year, he cannot be prosecuted by the provincial authorities. It is the practice in Ontario not to give a man a new license if he has infringed the law in the previous year, so that the provincial authorities will have to inquire of the Dominion authorities whether or not he has been convicted under the Dominion regulations. I would like to know how many overseers are going to be appointed by the Dominion government on the Georgian bay.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: One at Parry Sound, one at Leith, one at Wiarton, one at Pene-tanguishene.

I said there would be three, apparently there are four. Then these seven fishery overseers are in the southeastern portion of the Georgian bay. That is altogether too many officials, three or four competent men would be quite sufficient. Thus it looks to me as if politics had something to do with these appointments. One of the main strengths of the fishery overseer is that the fishermen look to him to exert his influence to lengthen the open season or shorten the close season, or hope to have him act as leniently as he can with reference to the enforcement of the fishery regulations. When this government had no fishery overseers the petitions of these men had to be transmitted to the government through the provincial overseer and it was to him that the fishermen looked for a reply. It looks as if these officers were being appointed by the Dominion government so that the information may be sent back not to a provincial official, but to a Dominion official. From whom has the minister had complaints that the provincial regulations have not been properly enforced?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not know whether the provincial regulations were enforced, but we know that ours have not been properly enforced in some cases.
Can the minister cite a single case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Oh, yes, I can cite many.
I can cite one. A short time ago I visited a fishing country and found leads of 550 feet being used, contrary to law, in Mitchell's bay.
Did the hon. gentleman advise the provincial authority?
Yes.
Did he take action?
Shortly after, but it had been going on for a year without being noticed.

That is a case where something was brought to the attention of the officer and he rectified it. That is all that could have been done by a Dominion official. There can be no argument for the appointment of these men and it would be in the interests of the fisheries not to have them appointed. Did the minister consult the Ontario government as to the necessity of appointing them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The law says that the fishery officers appointed under the Act are the ones to have authority to enforce the Act. There must have been violation of the law, but there has never been any return to us of money collected as fines, while the law provides that all money so collected must be turned in to the Receiver General for Canada.
Have you applied to the province for it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Oh, yes, we have.

The minister admits that he has not communicated with the provincial authorities to find out whether they have been enforcing the Dominion regulations, although he is willing to forego his right to fishery licenses. Has he intimated to the provincial authorities that he was going to appoint 40 Dominion officers, and asked them if they thought it was necessary or whether the provincial officers would perform the duties which the 40 Dominion officers are about to perform.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I must admit that I have not asked the provincial authorities whether they would advise me if these officers should be appointed or not, because I thought it was our duty to do it ourselves. So long as we were satisfied that there were violations of the law and that these violations were detrimental to the fisheries, we
thought it was our duty to prevent such violations. The provincial authorities have their own officers to look after their own regulations concerning licenses, but it is our duty to see to the observance of our own regulations. As to violations of the-law I might mention the Killarney case, a very flagrant case, referred to in the report of the Georgian Bay Commission. In view of these facts we are not going to beg of the Ontario government to carry out our regulations. It is our duty to see that they are properly observed, for fear that we may afterwards be charged with not having performed our duty. I feel I would have been derelict in my duty if I had not adopted this course.

Does the minister not think that the provincial officials going over the same ground, could, without any additional labour, perform the duties which will be performed by these 40 officers to be appointed by this government^

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But once more, my hon friend-

I quite understand that what the minister wants is the enforcement of the regulations of his department by his own officials. But he tells us that he is in perfect harmony with the provincial authorities, yet he has given the provincial government no chance to come to an agreement with him on this point, he has not consulted with them as to the appointment of these officials. And I do not see why something should not have been done along that line.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: One point, perhaps, I did not make very clear. The officers appointed toy the Ontario government, of course, receive instructions from the provincial authority, and these instructions must refer to the provincial laws and regulations. For the enforcement of our regulations, we must give those who are to enforce them specific instructions, but how can we give instructions to these provincial officers? We have no authority over them, and they would profoaibly tell us so. I expect that the men whom we appoint will see to it that our regulations are observed, while the provincial officers will especially look after the regulations in relation to issuing of licenses and matters under the authority of the provincial government.

But could not the minister appoint these provincial officials to carry out the regulations of the Dominion? _ If that suggestion were made to the provincial authorities, I have no doubt they would agree to it. There would be no confusion and one corps of officers would carry out the two sets of regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I would rather have our system than one under which a large number of officers are appointed. We have suffered in some (provinces by this system of appointing guardians and overseers at such small salaries that they could not be expected to devote their time to the work. But we appoint fewer men, pay them salaries that will cover all their time, and look to them for results.
What will the 40 men with all their paraphernalia cost?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Five hundred dollars for each man.
Twenty thousand dollars per annum on a little question of dignity.

The point the minister raises is one of those that could have been amicably arranged between the two governments. If the number of officials is too large, and the salaries too small, an agreement could have been made to follow rather the plan that he thinks best.

How does the minister expect that these men are going to devote their whole time to the work for the money he speaks of-$500 per annum each? These men, if they are going to perform their duties, must Ibe away from home a good deal, travelling u,p and down the river. I suppose each will have to pay his own living expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: His living expenses, when he is out, will be paid by the department.
Then the minister did not give us the facts correctly. He said these men would cost $500 each per annum which-
You asked what the salary was.	.

No, the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) asked what these men would cost, and the minister said $500 per iannum each. But now the minister says their expenses must be paid while they are out, and it is clear they must be out every day, for the men along the river have small nets which they will use in an effort to evade the law. The Ontario government men are running up and down the river in their little gasoline launches all the time. I have seen them come along where men were trying to spear fish at night. How much will the minister allows these officers of his for living expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We pay the actual disbursements. That is the custom that has always been followed in the department.
I suppose you will furnish each man wish a gasoline boat?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Where necessary, but not in all cases.

How is a man going to watch the fisheries unless he is out on the river? Such a man must have a gasoline launch, and it must be a fast one too, because the men who are fishing illegally generally have pretty fast little launches themselves. The running of the launch and the living expenses of the men will iadd at least $2 a day while they are travelling around-the expenses will probably be more than the salary. Instead of $500 each, these men will cost $1,000 each. That is, $40,000 is to be paid by this government quite unnecessarily. The only point that the minister makes, it seems to me, i3 that the Ontario officials have not authority to carry out his regulations. But, if the minister would have an order in council passed that the fishery officers appointed by the local government should have power to enforce the Dominion regulations, he could save this $40,000 per annum. Am I not right in understanding it that way?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No.
Then, will the minister explain.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: These men would not be under our control or subject to our instructions. It would foe a system absolutely detrimental to the fisheries. The hon. gentlemen (Mr. Reid, Grenville) seems to be surprised at an expenditure of $40,000 in connection with these fisheries. These fisheries in Ontario are very important.
No doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: And I say that spending a sum of even $40,000 for the .preservation of those fisheries would not be an extravagant expenditure. I think it worth while to expend that amount of money to make sure that the fisheries shall be well preserved.
The issue I take with the minister is that it is not necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is a difference of opinion.

The minister states that these fishery overseers have no jurisdiction, and could not carry out his instructions. As I understand'it, the only instructions he could give them, would be the official regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Not only the official regulations, but there are a great number of specific instructions, which we have to give, and how could we do that to officers over whom we have no control ?

Has the hon. gentleman never heard of a station master at a union

station, who obeys the orders of several railway companies, and he only draws one salary ?
Is the minister going to make any appointments in the province of Manitoba ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We have one inspector and several overseers in Manitoba. It is not intended to increase the number.
Where are they located ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The inspector is at Selkirk; there is one overseer on Lake Manitoba and some on Lake Winnipegosis.
Are any of those additional officers you are providing for, going to be located in Manitoba ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries

speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to collect any license fees from the fishermen in Ontario ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The matter has been considered by the department, but no decision has been reached whether we should issue licenses in Ontario or not. We hope some day there will be an agreement, and we do not want to complicate the Question.

Will the minister state why the fishermen in British Columbia have to pay licenses to both governments, while in Ontario, they get off with a license to one government ? Notwithstanding what the minister said about the importance of the Ontario fisheries, the revenue collected by his department in that province was only $1,520 last year, while in the smaller province of British Columbia, the amount collected from the fishermen -was $41,000. It seems to me there is a discrimination which should not be continued, and that the money of the fishermen of British Columbia should not be taken to pay the salaries of those supernumerary overseers in Ontario, because that is what it will look like to them, when they find a difference of $40,000 between the revenues of the two provinces, and 40 new men are to be put on in Ontario to absorb this whole $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
This sum of $1,520 which the hon. gentleman speaks, must represent penalties which we have collected. We do not collect anything in the way of licenses for the Teasons I have just explained. But we are expending a large amount of money in British Columbia, much more than we are spending in On-121
tario. This amount under discussion is for the purpose of providing for the fishery protection service in British Columbia. Outside of that, we maintain several ships for the protection of the fisheries; we have also a large number of gasoline launches, and small boats for the same purpose. So the money expended for fishery protection in British Columbia does not compare with the amount spent in Ontario.

The point the minister has not touched is this: I have a large number of fishermen in my constituency, and when I go to them they demand an accounting from me as to why they are taxed $5 a year, and their brother fishermen in Ontario are not taxed at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken; the fishermen in both provinces are taxed. But in Ontario the money is collected by the provincial authorities, while in British Columbia it is collected by the Dominion authorities. Lately the provincial government saw fit also to put a tax upon the fishermen by imposing a new. license. Formerly, there was only one license, that imposed by the Dominion.

The minister still has not met my point. In British Columbia there are two licenses exacted from the fishermen, one by the provincial government and one by the Dominion government. In Ontario there is a license by the provincial government, but none collected by the Dominion government. So we have two licenses to pay, while in Ontario, there is only one license to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
That is in virtue of an especial agreement we made with the two provinces. After the judgment of the Privy Council we made an agreement with the British Columbia government by which we were to continue to protect the fisheries, to maintain the hatcheries, at the same time to administer the whole business, and also to collect the licenses, with the understanding however, that a certain portion of the amount which we collected was to be paid back to the provincial authorities. If I remember right, the amount voted last year by this parliament that we paid to the provincial authorities was $56,000 in virtue of that agreement. In Ontario an agreement was made that the province should collect the fees, _ pending a settlement of the fishery question. In the maritime provinces we continue to collect the licenses; in Quebec we collect the licenses in a portion of the province, and the provincial authorities collect them in another portion. But since we have made this agreement with the British Columbia government, the provincial authorities have seen fit to issue licenses themselves. They may



have had a right to do so, I do not say, it was a violation of the agreement which was made, but I think it would have been just as well to leave the situation untouched, and not to impose another license upon the fishermen. They could have left the matter in the hands of the Dominion authorities, until it had been definitely settled. But my hon. friend cannot find fault with the Dominion government for having continued to carry out the agreement which existed before. We claim that there is a part of British Columbia over which the provincial authorities have no jurisdiction. I mean the three-mile limit, and we claim that the right to issue licenses within the three-mile limit belongs exclusively to the Dominion authorities. That is a matter which is before the courts and of course, we will have the point settled by the decision which will be rendered.
I think the minister has not yet met my position, which is why his department collects licenses in British Columbia, while it collects no license in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is in virtue of the agreement which was made with the provincial government after the judgment of the Privy Council was rendered. An agreement was made in Ontario that they should collect the licenses, and with British Columbia and the maritime provinces that we should collect the licenses. Now, to our great surprise, the provincial government of British Columbia goes to work and passes laws taking power to issue licenses itself. In British Columbia we are under very large expense for the preservation of the fisheries. I suppose my hon. friend vrould think it only fair and right that as we are spending so much money for the preservation of the fisheries in British Columbia we should have some revenue out of them. The provincial government maintains one hatchery, but the most important hatcheries are maintained by us. The fishery protection service is maintained by the Dominion authorities. We have several ships that we are maintaining there for the protection of the fisheries, and I think it is only fair and just that we should issue these licenses for the purpose of meeting at least a portion of the expenses of protecting the fisheries. The situation is not the same in Ontario. There we do not maintain a fleet as we do in British Columbia. If the provincial government has seen fit to impose another tax upon the fisherman, I have no fault to find with it, as it simply exercises the power that it has to issu.e licenses and collect a fee. That is a question that the provincial authorities will have to discuss with the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries

speechtext: Perhaps my English is defective, but the minister has altogether avoided the point I tried to make. I have no fault to find with the expenditure in British Columbia. I think it his duty to make that expenditure, and that he is trying very hard to make the expenditure effective, but I am speaking just for the moment from the standpoint of the licensed fishermen in my riding, who are taxed five dollars a year, while their contemporaries in Ontario are taxed nothing at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, they are taxed in Ontario, too.
Well, they are taxed by the provincial government, but I am speaking of the federal taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Is the provincial government spending for the purpose of the fisheries the money which it collects from these fishermen? is it not true that almost all the money that is spent there is spent by the federal authorities?

The minister "has discussed the fishery policy of the British Columbia government with the ministers of that government, and I think they are quite able to take care of themselves, so it is not necessary for me to appear here as their champion. I will leave their case to themselves. But I would like to put on the records the contributions from the several provinces, as the subject has been mentioned. I have it here in the Auditor General's Report, at page 0-204, and it is as follows:
