One province contributes just about sixty per cent. It seems to me that an injustice is being done to the fishermen of that province, inasmuch as they are so heavily taxed as to pay sixty per cent of the whole fisheries revenue of Canada, while all the other eight provinces and a couple of unorganized districts contribute only the other forty per cent. I do not think the minister has met that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Well, take the case of Nova Scotia. The fisheries in which the Nova Scotia fishermen engage are mostly

those on the Grand Banks. The results of those fisheries are included in the reports which my hon. friend will see as to the yield of the fisheries in Nova Scotia. We could not very -well issue licenses to go and fish on the Grand Banks. Sir Charles Tup-per introduced a law soipe years ago under which fishermen going on the Grand Banks should receive a 'bounty. In British Columbia most of the fisheries are on the Fraser, and the other rivers in which they catch salmon. Fishing there is carried on in a different way from the method pursued ir. Nova Scotia, and that is the reason why there is a difference.

I see I cannot budge the minister on that point, but I would like to call his attention to another matter of some importance in connection with the fisheries protection service in British Columbia. About three years ago, when the government had its dispute with the British Columbia government, and when the two sets of officers were first put on. the minister issued licenses to a number of fishermen along the Fraser river, giving them certain rights, as they supposed. While they were exercising those rights they were interfered with by other fishery protection officers acting the same as the minister's own officers, in the name of the King. These men should not be subjected to any penalties from any quarter for doing anything which they were licensed to do in His Majesty's name, but they were brought before the courts by the provincial inspectors, subjected to heavy losses, fined and their occupation interfered with to a considerable extent in the height of the fishing season. These men naturally looked to the government, whom they had paid so handsomely for their licenses, to protect them from any of the consequences of the exercise of the power granted by those licenses. They have received no satisfaction whatever from this government, not even a sympathetic response, but merely a heartless declaration that this injury was not inflicted upon them by the federal authority, but that it was inflicted upon them by the provincial authority, and that, therefore, they must look to the province for compensation. I submit that is not the proper attitude for a federal department to take. It is not for me to say whether the federal government or the provincial government were in the right. To my mind that question should not be raised as regards the individual fisherman. The only correct course to take would be for the federal government to protect the holders of its licenses, to compensate them for any loss they met with through relying upon those licenses, and then in turn the federal government should look to the provincial government for compensation if compensation is due. Does 121 i
the minister not think that as a matter of right this government should protect the holders of its licenses?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We undoubtedly have the right to issue licenses in British Columbia as in other provinces, and to make laws and regulations concerning the fisheries. The provincial government was authorized by the legislature to issue licenses and they requested the fishermen to take provincial licenses. The provincial government undertook at the same time to pass regulations in connection with the fisheries and the fishermen of British Columbia thought the provincial government had no right to do that. The provincial government did not dispute the right of the federal government to issue licenses.
That is the very point; the authority given by the federal license was put in question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not think so.

The point was this:	The Dominion regulations
permitted the fishermen to carry on their calling during certain hours, and the provincial regulations provided certain different hours, and it wras because the fishermen were found fishing in the hours permitted by the Dominion but forbidden by the province that they w'ere brought to court. These men vrere fined for fishing at a time when the Dominion license told them they could fish.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: They were prosecuted because they were violating the provincial regulations, in that some of them did not take licenses as the provincial law prescribed. The fishermen fought the question in the courts, and though the question before the court was whether the provincial government had the right to make these regulations or not, I thought we should be generous enough to extend some help to these poor fishermen contending against a wealthy province. It was not because the province questioned our right to issue licenses, about which there is no doubt, but because the men were violating a provincial regulation, that they were prosecuted. In the first instance we got a lawyer to follow the case which was won by the fishermen, and on appeal to the high court that judgment was sustained. I should think it was ,a case in which the provincial government should pay the costs of the fishermen, but as they refused I thought it was only justice that we snould reimburse them their costs.
Was the payment of the costs made recently?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We paid the court charges.
I think the minister is in error; they never were paid their costs.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Claims were made by some of the fishermen for loss of time, but of course, we could not pay such. As a friend of the fishermen, my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) should commend us for having reimbursed them their costs. Not only that, but we are now before the Supreme Court to argue the stated case in which is involved the question of the three-mile limit.

I am delighted to hear that from the minister, but I am afraid he does not mean all he says. If he is really going to pay the fishermen all their costs, that is all I have been asking him to do, but that has not been done yet.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We paid all the court charges and the hon. gentleman should not press us to do more. If the fishermen have any claim for loss of time it should be paid by the provincial government which instituted the proceedings, and I am sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) with hisMn-fluence and prestige can get the provincial government to do that.
Unfortunately for the fishermen my commission is not to the provincial but to the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I know my hon. friend has great influence with the provincial government.

My point is, that the federal government should look to the provincial government for reimbursement as it is the federal government that ought to protect the holders of its licenses. The minister was a little in error about what is done with the fisheries revenue collected from British Columbia, when he said that part of it is by arrangement paid over to the provincial government. True, there was an arrangement several years ago when the decision of the Privy Council was first given, and under a modus vivendi the federal government was to continue to collect the license fees and remit one-half to the provincial government. What went wrong with that arrangement I do not know. But I do know that this government for some reason did not carry it out, and did not pay to the provincial government the part they agreed to pay; and it was in consequence of their failure to pay that amount during five or six years that the provincial government eventually took control of the situation by issuing regulations and imposing a license fee which from that time on they have collected. If this government had stuck to the modus vivendi, there would Mr. BRODEUR.
never have been any difficulty between them and the province of British Columbia, but one authority or the other would have imposed the license fee and divided it with the other government. The minister seems to be under the impression that that is going on now, but such is not the case, as I understand. I understand that this government is under no obligation to pay any part of the revenue which it collects to_the provincial government, and 1 would not like it to go on record that British Columbia was getting something which is not coming to us.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: After the judgment of the Privy Council there was an agreement that we should reimburse the government of British Columbia for some of the license fees collected if it transpired that we had not the right to issue such licenses. For many years no claim was made by the provincial authorities. But finally they made a claim, and we tried to determine what the amount of the claim was. There was a great divergence of opinion as to the basis of settlement, as to what should constitute the cost of administration. There was one contention on our part and another on the part of the provincial government. After a couple of years of discussion, we reached a settlement, and in the meantime the provincial government notified us that they wanted to put an end to the modus vivendi; and last year, after we had reached a settlement as to the amount that should be paid, the money was voted by parliament, and it has since been paid to the provincial authorities.

_ I would like to ask if the minister's attention was called to a report in the daily press the other day, of wholesale poaching on the west bank of Vancouver island, and of complaints that the protection service given there is altogether inadequate. Is any part of this money which we are now asked to vote for the purpose of strengthening that service, and, if so, in what respects is it to be strengthened?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Not only part, but all of this money is for the purpose of affording better protection to the fisheries on the western coast of the Island of Vancouver. The poaching my hon. friend refers to has been reported to the department in different ways, and it has been brought specially to my attention by my colleague, the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Temple-man) who urged very strongly upon me the advisability of providr'ng more boats for the protection of our fisheries, and this vote is for that purpose.
What nature of boats is this to provide?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give my hon. friend privately all the informa-

tion as to what we are going to do; but I think it would perhaps be better that the poachers should not know.

That is a very smooth answer of the minister, and I am very much obliged to him for the offer; but I am afraid that he cannot keep his boats so private that the poachers will not learn what he is doing almost as soon as his officials do; because I can tell him that the men engaged in poaching in opr ^waters have the very fastest boats that money can supply them with, and he must be very alert, indeed, to keep up with them. Up to the present our so-called fishery protection boats have been a laughing stock to the poachers. They know in advance the proposed movements of these boats, and every time a vessel of our protective fleet is due to approach, they are able to move in the opposite direction. I do not think that an apprehension or conviction of a poacher occurs once in a year, although scores of boats are poaching there all the time. No doubt these facts are known to the minister, but I mention them so that thev may be placed on record, and perhaps act as a stimulus to the department to do a little more than it has been doing to bring to an end a state of affairs which is almost ruining our fisheries. I would also like to ask whether any part of this vote is for t|ie protection of the fisheries on Puget Sound in connection with the regulations under the International Fisheries Treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No. I may say that the treaty is not yet in force. It has not yet been passed by the United States authorities. When I was in Washington some days ago, I took up the question with the United States government, and the Secretary of State intended to advise the President to request the passage of the necessary legislation as soon as possible. I do not know whether that has been done yet or not. This vote is entirely for the protection of the fisheries on the west coast of the Island of Vancouver. If the necessity arises for the protection of the fisheries on Puget Sound, that will be attended to.

Of course, the protection of the fisheries on Puget Sound is a matter of joint arrangement between the two countries; and if the fishery regulations, which are now overdue, are proclaimed simultaneously in both countries, it will be necessary for us to have our arrangements for protection ready, otherwise the season will pass with our fisheries there at the mercy of fishermen from the American side.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Provision is made for that in our main estimates. This vote is only to make provision from now to the ifirst of April.
Does the minister rely altogether on the Americans for the inspection of their traps, or will there be Canadian boats also for police duty?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Of course, we have to rely on the American authorities, because under the treaty the carrying out of the regulations on each side of the line must be carried out by the authorities of each country.

The minister has a regulation in regard to the export of fish. Will that be carried out under his inspection, or are the Americans under any arrangement to assist in keeping our fish out of their markets?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The fishery regulations for preventing the exportation of fish in order to preserve the fisheries are certainly going to be attended to by this government.
The minister has no intention of making any other regulations this year with regard to the exportation of fish than the regulations in force last year, and for some years previous?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We have not considered any change in the regulations in connection with that.

I ask that because I observe in the arrangement recently under discussion here that there is to be a free interchange of fish between the two countries, and that there is also an engagement on the part of Canada that no regulations of any kind will conflict with this offer of the free interchange of fish. Of course we have induced the American government to take off the duty on fish in the expectation that they will get oiflr salmon to use in their canning factories, and they would regard it as a violation of our promise not to have any conflicting regulation, if the minister maintained his prohibition of export. This matter ought to be clearly understood, because it is important to our fishermen to know well in advance if they are to be permitted to export their catch during the present season. They are advised by the arrangement we have recently been discussing that they will be permitted to export while the minister's regulations provide that they will not be permitted. We have here the two ministers concerned in what seems to be a conflicting arrangement, and I think it would be well to have an authoritative statement, so that men on the Fraser who are so vitally interested should be advised as early as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is nothing in the arrangement which interferes with the right of the Canadian Fisheries Department to

make any regulation which may be deemed necessary for the protection of the Canadian fisheries, and in like manner the American government will be free to make any regulation that seems reasonably necessary for the protection of their fisheries. That is the general state of the situation. What would be the effect of any particular regulation that might arise would have to be considered. I can only state the general principle governing the arrangement.

I am sorry to hear that, because that was one feature of the arrangement at Washington that pleased me, that we were to have free interchange of fish. It was a matter I had urged on the House during the three sessions I have been here. I have always thought that the exportation of fish should not be prohibited, as it is by order in council, and I read in the agreement from Washington that no regulation shall be made or maintained which unreasonably hampers the more liberal exchange of commodities now proposed. It seems to me quite clear that the prohibition of the export of fish does unreasonably hamper the interchange of this commodity, and that it would be so held. It seems to me the ministers would do well to take council together on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am content to state the general principle. As to how it shall apply in this particular case I must leave the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to study that out for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that this regulation has been put on the statute-book for the purpose of protecting our fisheries, and if I remember rightly such a provision was unanimously recommended by the British Columbia Commission which sat some years ago, and on which all interests were represented. It was unanimously recommended that this was a measure necessary to protect our fisheries. It is a regulation of local concern for the special purpose of protecting our fisheries, and we may exercise in respect to it the same right as we do with regard to licenses.

If that interpretation is carried out it puts us in this position, that an arrangement has been made for the free exchange of fish, and that under that we are bound to admit all the American fish offered to us in competition with the catch of our own fishermen, while under the regulations made bv the Fishery Department those same fishermen are prohibited from passing their fish across to the canners on the American si'de, which I think is a condition most unfair to the fishermen.
Mr. FIELDING

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would be a matter entirely under our control, of course.
Immigration, amount required for seed grain and relief advances, $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This amount is asked for to meet requirements which have arisen hy reason of the unfavourable nature of last season in the southwestern part of the western provinces. The season was very dry, and the crops short, and so far as our information goes there are about 4,000 homesteaders who are short of seed grain. Seed grain has been supplied in the past under similar circumstances, and it is understood to be the policy of the country that where people are in occupation of land in the west, of which they have not acquired the ownership, so that they can raise money on it as security to buy grain, the government will make advances, taking a lien upon the land as security for those advances. The government does not make a gift of the grain; it makes an advance of the grain to the farmer, and, being the only authority that is able to take a lien upon his land, takes that lien as security for the advance. We are afraid we will have to ask for more than $50,000, but $50,000 is sufficient for the purchases that will have to be made now, so that the grain will be ready for distribution at the beginning of the season. We may have to ask for a further sum in the supplementary estimates for the coming year.
How does the minister estimate the quantity? Has he reports from his officers or does he judge by the applications from farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was known, of course, last summer, that the crop was short in that part of the country. The immigration branch has had officials, from time to time, go through the country and size up the situation. Also, of course, we have received a large number of applications. But we depend rather on the investigations of our officers. Of course, there are many people who are apt to leave off making an application until the time they need the grain, and so, between now and the spring, we may expect applications to come in of which we have not heard. But we have, as far as possible, covered the area affected by the drought and believe we have made a fair estimate of the requirements.
For the three provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, we are not taking any action with regard to Manitoba so far as I am aware. In Manitoba, as my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) knows, in the part where the shortage occurred, the land has practically all been patented, and so there does not exist the position of which I have spoken in which the Dominion government

is the only authority that can take security .against the land. We are not touching cases in any of the provinces in which the land has passed out of the hands of the Dominion government. In such cases, we feel, the settler is in a position to make provision for himself, or the provincial government is the authority that should undertake the responsibility.

Would the minister mind specifying the district to be covered. He speaks of four thousand homesteaders to be supplied. I do not think that $50,000 will cover, or anything like cover, what is necessary to supply so many. How much seed does he propose to allow?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the moment, I can only outline the district in a general way. It is particularly, south of the Canadian Pacific railway main line and west of the Sault line, that is, it is in southwestern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. It is quite true, and I have already said, that the amount we are asking for now is not all that will be required, but we think it is sufficient to carry us through the present fiscal year. As I have said, we shall have to ask for a further sum in the supplementary estimates for the coming fiscal year.
I notice that this is for relief advances also. Is there necessity for relieving farmers in distress?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There has been, I am sorry to say, some necessity, and some advances have been made-not on a large scale, but there have been cases in which we felt it was needed in the general interest and that something .might be done so that suffering might be avoided.
Does the department look to the individual farmer for repayment or to the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We collect direct from the individual. On the occasion of the seed grain advances of two or three years ago, the .advances were made to the provincial government, though we handled the actual distribution. The provincial government dealt with the farmers wlho held their patents, and collected from the farmers, and we collected .from the provincial government. But in all cases where the farmer has not received his patent, he is not in a position to give security to any other authority than the Dominion government. In such cases, the Dominion government deals direct with the homesteader.

What has been the experience in the past as to repayment of these
advances? Have repayments been made promptly?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may give a few figures on that subject. Advances were made in the years 1886, 1887, 1888, 1890, 1894, 1895, 1896, total amount advanced was $4,660.08, and in 1908 the total amount advanced was $401,621.76. The aggregate of these advances for all the years named was $745,303.05. Of that total $549,858.56 has been repaid. The remainder, $195,444.49, is still outstanding. Six per cent interest \vas charged on advances before 1900, and since then 5 per cent has been charged. I think, under all the circumstances, the repayments have been made fairly promptly. We do not press the settler for payment. We hold a lien against his land, and when he applies for his patent the patent is issued to him, but the lien is inscribed on the face of the patent. Whenever he wishes to dispose of his land, or raise money on it, this lien must be paid off before he can complete the transaction. We find that effective in securing repayment, and, inasmuch as we are receiving 5 per cent on the advances, we have never pressed settlers for repayment. The result, I think, is a fairly satisfactory statement.
Does that cover patented as well as unpatented lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Only the unpatented. We have made no advances on patented lands except through and on the responsibility of the provincial government.
I presume that, in the case of relief advances, a lien is made?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes; it is the same.
This whole question, I suppose, is being watched by the officials of the Immigration Department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And I presume they receive information from the mounted police and from other settlers, the people watching to see that there is no suffering?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, the severity of the winter and the conditions have been such that we cannot guarantee that there have been no cases of suffering. But, so far as it has been possible and reasonable, we have done what could be done to prevent any serious cases of suffering. We believe we have done very good work and have not unduly burdened the resources of the country.
